div.p: Ad AI IfA A, I A{.l A• A A A MAKES VEE EL)I.I A. 14 PATENT bh1,14.M A BEST PASTRY,
ILLUSTRATED FASITIONS

There is a very pretty style of work which is much in vogue at present, and employed both for the adornment of dresses and underskirts alike. This is Madeira worked taffetas, and it is equally effective for costumes and petticoats. A. very charming costume had the entire skirt and bodice covered with thia work, inSerspersed with lace applique, and was expressed in a delicsite tone of green taffetas embroidered with white, ruffles of delicate lace gracing the threat and wrists. Green and white is a combination much affected by the French modistes, and there is undoubtedly a pleasingness in the union of the two ,colonrs which must satisfy the most fastidious 'taste.

The pretty tailor-made costume sketched is cut in the latest and most approved mode, and is noticeable for its lack of shoulder seams, and the fact that it owns to a basque at the back. It is expressed in fine navy - blue serge piped with bright red satin at alllhe seams, while the same contrasting note of colour is continued in the collar and cuffs. The latest 'novelty in regard to tailor- tuades is the method of setting the sleeves into the shoulder, the usual seam being absent. Ladies' tailors, as a rule, gght shy. of any °litre mode, and in spite of the many and somewhat bewildering ,•arieties of sleeves patronized by the modistes, the '-, tailors seem +content with a modification of

div.head: PnETTY TAILOR-MADE.
div.p: A PnETTY TAILOR-MADE.

site Ilshihap sleeve, the fulness at the wrist being obtained by goring and shaping set into a military cuff or a plain band. The bell sleeve is also fashionable, but • one cannot but admit that the plainer and more severe the cut of a tailor-made gown the greater its success. The basqued bodice seems to have been accepted for the meantime and has settled down into its place as one of the season's novelties. It appears in many and various forms. The two which are perhaps the prettiest, and therefore the most fashionable, are the pos- tillitm tails behind, and the very long Louis XV. coat tails ornamented with handsome brilliant or enamelled buttons. The bolero has by no meam disappeared from our midst, for there is no doubt that it has made a place for itself in the realms of dress. There is a smartness about it that is un• deniable, and it is such a portable little outdoor wrap that womankind realize its good qualitio and refuse to give it up. At the same time onE occasionally encounters some horrible unsightly garments, ill-fitting to a degree, that pass under the name of bolerokwhich are enough to make ons pause,before commuting one's self to an order far this style of coat.
The dainty blouse depicted is made in pale blue crystalline trimmed with ecru lace both am iataertrion and as appliqued medallion% A few

div.head: DAINTY BLOUSE.
div.p: A DAINTY BLOUSE.

tucks, which seem part and parcel of all dress just now, are effectively introduced on the bodice and sleeves. There is a very lovely lace which is used very much at present on both blouses and dresses, namely, luxemil de so', which makes an extremely effective trimming. This is generally used on fine silky materials such as taffetas or anon de soie. Rougher materials such as serge or holland are trimmed with linen lace or a sort of fine raffia. Dress at present is altogether elaborate, and not only ar• there multitudinous tuckings, gatherings, and hand embroideries, but braidings of all kinds, wide and narrow, in wool, silk, chenille, or tinsel, some of the smartest gowns being alto- gether covered with an all-over design in fine corded braid. The very fact that braidings are so much ex eridenee at present is sufficient te proclaim their speedy banishment from the toilettes of the leaders of fashion, for whatever becomes generally adopted is soon considered elietode by the ultra fashionable.
The charming ,hat illustrated is of the latest vogue, and has acme straight from Paris. It is of deep corn-coloured or coffee straw trimmed

div.head: CHARMING HAT.
div.p: A CHARMING HAT.

with black, with a bunch of bright pink gera- niums at the back on the hair. This is le dernier en i from across the Channel, and the effect is always smart. French femininity have a most wonderful art of arranging the coiffure and putting on the hat at just the correct and most becoming angl which few Englishwomen possess. It is jhst this which makes all the difference in a woman's appearance, for even those who get their clothes from quite the test places appear dowdier than their less expensively.clad but cleverer sisters. It is the woman who makes the clothes a success usually and not (as is two often supposed) the clothes the woman. The long pendant bows so much in vogue here have been declared bad form in Paris, and it is, therefore, probable that they will soon disappear from our midst.

The newest veilings this season are very pretty and varied. One of the most becoming is of fine mechlin net, with alternate chevrons of white and black pin spots, while large, black velvet pastilles are arranged at greater intervals. There is a strong tendency towards black and white veil nets, and the fine net grounds with irregular patterns of spots are newer than the -open Russian nets.
COQUETTS.

div.head: WOMEN'S CHAT.
div.p: WOMEN'S CHAT.

Coronation chaos abounds everywhere along the route of the pageant. Everywhere carpenters and builders are erecting small or huge stands according to the avail- able frontage, and what with th 3 noise of the hammer. the flying sawdust, the ladders of the painters and illuminators, it is difficult to pass comfortably along man 7 of the street. It has, at any rate, cured many people of the superstition of passing under ladders.stece frequently no other choice is open to the pedestrian. Seats appear to be selling fairly well at moierate priers, and every point of advantage is being utilised for gain- ing profit in this way. The great idea seems to be for making money, but Royal displeasure is not unlikely t.e fall upon those Society folks who are letting out their London houses with this one object in view. Several of the great houses on the other band have been placed at the King's disposal fer the Coronation guests. Wimborne House will be occupied by Prince and Princess Henry of IPrussia,whilst the Grand Duke &mitre and the Duchess Elizabeth of Russia will stay at Chesterfield Rouge. The latest portrait of the Queen is a charming picture of her Majesty, in company with the little Princess Victoria of Wales, and the Ladies Alexandra and Maud Duff. The Queen looks almost as young as ever, and no one would imagine her to be the grandmother of the three sturdy children, the eldest of whom, Lady Alexandra Duf, has just entered upon her twelfth year. The little Princess Victoria of Wales—this title no longer applying to the King's danghter—is the prettiest of the children of :he Prince and Princess of Wales, and looks quite as strong and robust as her cousins the Ladies Duff. Much :importance has been attached to athletic training in the bringing up of the Fife children, and the Ladies Alexandra and Maud are both expert little swordswomen. Their mother, the Duchess, of Fife, is devoted to them, superintending all the little details in their daily life, and is very seldom separated from her children. The Royal garden party, which will be one of the principal entortainmente for the Coronation gueits, is to take place at Windsor en July Ist. The King and Royal party will go by rail to Slough, driving thence through Eton to ths Castle. The giving of the party at Windsor,instead of at Buckingham Palace will necessi- tate the large number of guests travelling down from London, but Windsor is incomparably better situated for a garden party, aed the !country will, at the end of this month be looking at its best. Given a fine clear day, there is no finer view in the Kingdom than is to be seen from the East Terrace, whilst the beauties and splendid appointments of Windsor Castle form a fitting background to the scene. Everything in convection with the Royal entertainment is to be on a magnificent scale and it will be one of the most memorable events of the Coronation festivities. With more genial weather, the House of Commons is once more becoming the fashionable meeting place for afternoon tea on the Terrace. The doctors continue to frown at the five o'clock dainties that find their way there, and into every fashionable drawing-room and they denounce these as being very much more injurious than the old fashioned bread and butter and cake meal. But the change is, at least, a pleasant one, and an long as Society exists, afternoon tea with its dainties and gossip is not likely to fall into disfavor. The en tout gas has, until very recently, quitejaken the place of the more elaborate parasol, an item which can scarcely puzzle us when we take the weather into consideration. The craze for black and white has ex tended to both, one parasol, likely to be conch in evi dence being of white chiffon frills edged with a tiny ruching of black chiffon ; another being built of white silk, appliqued with !prays and garlands of black Chantilly lace. All the best parasols are lined with gauged chiffon, or lac, and the handles are no Imager eccentric, being of the neat useful variety, balls pre- dominating. The chire permed will prcb ably enjoy a wide, though brief vogue. It is fatally easy of imita- tion, and though this is supposed to be a desirable fern, of flattery, well-dressed women invariable fail to appre- ciate meeting cheap copies of their modes, at every

turn. The mew elan) which fastens on to the belt, and at the other end of the more or less elabcrate chain, grasps a handlcerchief. is not likely to be long appreciated siave by the girls of the working class, who by such mean. will be enabled to exhibit a kerchief of many bright hues, and the individual who profession it is, to annex other people's goods. At the moment smart women are utilising these clasps beautifully jewelled, and together with a dainty lace handkerchief, these form a desirable haul for one of the light-fingered gentry. None of the dev'cee which are always cropping up to take the place of pockets are a success, and as yet modistes show no sign' of relenting, and allowing the smallest receptacle to be nlaced in our gowns. Flowers real, imitation, or hand-painted abound. Evening gowns and wraps chew knots and trails of them, headgear is almost hidden beneath a wealth of bloom ard foliage, and on fans, and fichus, flowers are being laid with a generous band. This craze has spread to fabrics. the majority of which are showing floral designs. In the millinery world, however, fruit will shortly take the place of flowers for a space. Fashion- able milliners are already showing Ws and toques trimmed with bunches of red and white currants, arid clusters of cherries ate likely to enjoy their annual vcgue. Vegetables, such as tiny carrots, and tomatoes are opt:uterine on up-tc-date headgear, but these should be avoided, since they have only their novelty to recom- mend them. With many fashionable brides, white lace mittens are taking the place of gloves, these being generally Brueeele applique, the ?reign, orange blnetsoms heather, and myrtle with true lovers' knots which are not too promi- nently treated. Such mit'ene bay.., of course many advantages ever gloves. In the first place they need lot be removed for the ceremony, they are cooler and more comfortable wear, and again they permit of a good view ofethe " magic circle," of which the average bride is particularly proud. Lives there a woman who le not familiar with line- rocksee' long cloths, rheetings. nainsonles, twills, and carnbries There must be very few, if any, for the name of this firm, which was established in 1791, has been banded down from mother to daughter ever since, as being the one upon which dependence coald be placed for the best of everything in this way. That Hnrrockses should have added flannelettes to their list of beautiful fabrics is therefore a matter which will rejoice the hearts of many. These flannelettes appear in the most exquisite of colourings, are by no means expensive, and moreover ere,aelabeolutely safe wear,as it is possible for flannelette to De. This latter item ice. light eon/lidera- Mew when nee takes into account the numbers of lives that have been lost, through the wearing of the danger- ou' varieties of flannelette. Bqrks especially designed for girl; reading are usually a failure. That seems to be the general opinion, after a long discussion on the subject in a literary journal, and there is little drubt that it is the correct view. There are a few writers who understand girls but, as a rule. those who write " books for girls " overlook the fact that girls and boys are mostly interested in the same cies,' of subject certainly girls arc just as much in- terested in tales of adventure as are boys and the best children's bncke do equally well for both sex's, and also make good reading for grown-up people.

div.head: EXAMINER, FRIDAY JUNE 6 1902
div.p: THE EXAMINER, FRIDAY JUNE 6 1902
LOCAL CASES AT LIVERPOOL

div.head: COUNTY SESSIONS.
div.p: COUNTY SESSIONS.

THEFT PROR SANKEY BOARD SCHOOL. 11 PRISONER'S EXTRAORDINARY HIERAYIOUR. Ttretiverpool County Intermediate Sessions was held on Tuesday at the Session House, Islington under the Chairmanship of Sir W B Forweod Edward Griffiths (3),shoemaker, and John Murphy 032),hawker, pleaded not galley to having, at Sankey, ,on the 3rd May,broken and entered the Sankey Board School, and stolen there- from an OESTRUS and a cape. The prisoners were discovered en the premises in the early hours of the morning by the police. During the hearing of the ease the prisoner Griffiths conducted himself in an extraerdinary manner, frequently interrupting the witnesses and UV:Off bad language. He told one of the witn that be did not know what he was saying—he was talking like electricity. A police sergeant who arrested the prisoners was questioned by Mr Harrison, who prosecuted, as to Griffiths' mental state, and replied that when apprehended Griffiths was quite rational, and he only now acted in the manner commented epon.—ThCury found both prisoners guilty. —Griffiths, when asked by the clerk if he admitted having been sentenced to six years' penal servitude at Durham Assizes, shouted out : " It's no use askieg me anything at all. I won't answer. ! "—The previous con- viction was proved. Murphy pleaded guilty to a pre- vious sonviction.—The magistrates sent both men to prison for three months with hard labour.—Griffiths snapped his fingers at the magistrates as he loft the dock.

A PERSISTENT TEIEF FROM NEWTON-LH-WILLOWS. John Boawell, alias Salomon Taylor (62), labourer, deadel guilty to haying at Newton-le-Willows, between the 15th and 17th April, stolen one tablecloth and two tea towel., the property of Lonis Forster. The Chair- man, in passing sentence, said that during the last 24 years the prisoner had spent most of his times prison, and always for petty thefts. There was no doubt he was a persistent thief, and one of those men society must get rid of. Seatence of alma calendar months with hard 'aborr was passed, Mr Oulton prosecuted. COWARDLY' ATTACK ON AN OLD MAN AT EIIESCOT. James Murphy (26), collier, and Matthew John Flynn (32). collier, were indicted with haying at Prescot on the 10th May assaulted James Dickie, with intent to rob him.--The prosecutor is as old man, and was attacked by the prisoners, who butted him in the stomach and kicked him, rendering him uneunseioas.—The prisoners were each sent to gaol for six months.__ _ _
THEFT OF A BICYCLE, AT_ WIDNES.

Geerge Henry Kennington (29), pleaded not guilty to leaving at Widnes, on the 26th April, stolen a bicycle, the property of George Lloyd. The ease as presented by Mr D'Arcy en behalf of the prosecution, was that the bicyclewss stolen from the outside of a public-house in Widnee. On the evening of the same day. prisoner was found in possession of it, sad he stated that he bad bought the machine for 31 from a TIM whom he did not know.—The jury found the prisoner guilt), bet recom- mended him to mercy.—The Chairman bowled him over to be of good behaviour for twelve monthd.
STEALTH* AND RECHIVING AT ST. HELENS.

Martin Mullins (22), labourer, was charged with baying broken late the shop of Solomon Duckworth, at St Helens, between May sth and 7th, and stealing there- from a quantity of clotbing,valued at abort £7. Joseph Leabey (22), was charged with receiving the same, knowing them to have been stolen. Tbe case for the prosecution was that both men had entered the house, and had together rod a portion of the stolen aseds. In his defence, Leabey denied having entered the house, and said the ether prisoner handed over some clothing to him to keep for a while. Leahav was sound guilty, and a sentence of six months' imprisonment was passed on each prisoner. Mr Morris prosecuted, and Mr Marshall and Mr Griffiths defended.

div.head: LOCAL LICENSING MATTERS. The Rebuilding of the Feathers Hotel.
div.p: LOCAL LICENSING MATTERS. The Rebuilding of the Feathers Hotel.

The special session for transferring licences was bold at the Borough Police Court, on Monday morning. The following members of the Licensing Committee sat on the Bench :—Mr F Monks (in the chair), Alderman Francomb, and Messrs J Geddes and T Birchen, whilst the other magistrates in attendance were Councillor Smethurst, and Mt sirs J Hayward, 9 Wright, and Thornton. Mr Stanley Wilson, the Deputy Town Clerk, applied on behalf of the Corporation for a final order confirming the provisional licence granted for the rebuilding of the Feathere Hotel, Bridge-street. In October, 1900, plans, prepared by Messrs William and Seger Owen, for the rebuilding of this hotel on an improved fsontage were passed. The premises bad been built in strict accord- ance with the plane, and all he had to de was to satisfy the Bench that that was so. lifr William Owen said the premises had been built is accordance with the plans which this Magistrates had approved, and for which they gave a provisional grant The Chief C3netable said he was satisfied as to that. The hotel was examined by the pones and was found to , be in exact accordance with the plane. The Chairman I bear the hotel has been bought by a public-house trust. The Chief Constable : That is so. We will watch that with great interest. The Chairman said he hoped it would he managed as well as one in Coalbroekdale, Shropshire, which was controlled by the fires with which he was connected. The house was kept in a most exemplary manner, and , was a very profitable enterprise. The application would be granted. The following transfers were granted : White Hart, Sankey-street, from Ann Brierley to Joseph Shilleock ; Bay Horse, Winwick-street, from Joseph Shilloock to John W Minton ; Causeway Hotel, Wilderspool-road from Arthur W Paul to Ephraim Aukland (jun); Griffin Inn, Horeemarket-street. from Mary 11 Wooletencroft to A W Paul ; off-licence, 1, Allen•street, from William , Alleock to William Charnock ; off-licence, 253,Winwick- , road, from Owen Jones to Mary Ellen Jones.—Mr laneworth, soliaitor, applied in the last case.

div.head: ALDERMAN ROBERTS AND WHITECROSS WARD.
div.p: ALDERMAN ROBERTS AND WHITECROSS WARD.
A Refutation and a Vote of Confidence.

At • meeting of the Whiteermis Ward Liberal Cent- mlttee, held on Friday night last week the following resolution was passed unanimously :—"That this meet- ing of the Whitecrose Ward desires to express its deep sympathy with Alderman Henry Roberts, regirdiag the untrue and vindictive statements which have recently illtxdared in a loaal publication, eoncerning his alleged rejection by the Ward Committee as its chairman; that, further, this meeting points to the fact of his appoint- ment as one of its vice-chairmen, as a refutation of the false statements referred te,and rejoices in his continued cc-operation with the Ward and assures him of its warm appreciation of his past services, and its unabated confidence in him personally and also in his public: life." I resolution of sympathy with the relatives of the late Mr Thema,' Hawtborn,who was a vice-chairman of the committee, was also passed.

The Town-Clerkship of St. Helens. At the meeting of the St. Helens Town Council en Wednesday afternoon, Alderman .J C Gamble proposed that th• vacancy in the town-clerkship be advertised at a salary of .E9oo,rising to £l,OOO at the end of one year. Alderman Forster proposed that Alderman Joseph Massey, who Was three years ago practically elected to the position, should be asked to take the town-clerkship. Mr Massey however, declined. Several members suggested that a much smaller salary would be sufficient, but the question was ultimately left in the hands of the Parliamentary Committee to arrange and report to the Council before they advertised.

BritannTa may rule the waves, but (observes the " Daily Chronicle ") she doss not rule them straight enough for the comfort of the Maharajah of Bhawalpur, who started from Karachi by sea to pay his respects to the King at his coronation. By the time he leached Bombay be was in two senses sick of the voyage, and decided that it was not worth while to face another fortnigbt on the sea. So he bas sent his apologies and respects by cable. He will now admire more than ever the courage that carries constant streams of suffering Englishmen to India when they might stay at home.

div.head: "BROKE IN OUR WARS."
div.p: "BROKE IN OUR WARS."
Ashton-in-Makerfield Soldier's Unhappy Experience.

Mr. John Holden, of 5, Ashton Cross, Asisten-in- Makerfield, Lsneashire, is one of these men who have been" broke in our wars," in the service of a country which is not over-generous towards them. Mr Holden is only thirty-four years of age, but as early as 1884 found him in the ranks of the Royal Welsh Fusiliers. In the following year his regiment was sent out to Burma to assist'Lord Roberts in - rlidating the Empire in

(JOHN HOLDEN'S 1t WARD FOR HIS SERVICES-) that quarter of the globe. He was bugler to General Whit*. He encountered the fatigues and dangers of campaigning in het and uncertain climates. Sometimes a march brought about nine or ten croisings of a river In a single day, and the men had to wade through the water fully dressed and were partiallerdried by tha sun between each wade: then the nights invariably pro duced very objectionable mists which caused a " clammy " feeling to descend upon the men. Holden luckily survived the fighting and succeeded in keeping disease at bay, at all events for the time being. "However, said he in relating his interesting story to a newspaper man, "when I returned to Lucknow, I was struck down by enteric fever, upon which the more dreaded smallpox followed. In 18811 I was invalided home with debility and wee reported to be medically unfit for further service. I was not content to rest under this order and it was not long before I was passed by the doctors and enabled to enlist with the 21st Huasare. Again I went out to India, where I arrived in January, 1891. Service in Madras is exces- sively trying to Europeans, and with others I was silt to the convalescent home at Wellirgton. in the bills, for eighteen months in order to get acclimatised and to prepare for a long spell in India. Artemis and rheuma- tism, the outcome of the Burma hardships, asserted themselves, and once more I was invalided home. Care- ful treatment at Canterbury, the depet of the 21st Hussars, followed by four months at an Eastberne convalescent home, only ended in my becoming hope- lessly worse, and, for the second time in my military career I was discharged as ' medically unfit for further service,' being given a pension of 61 a day for twelve months, and at the and of twelve months the War Office thought that their obligations towards me had been fully met ! ' e When he joined the army he was 11 stone 81b. ; when he was discharged after eleven ware foreign service be•was 7 stone 41b. Holden continued in this plight for a long period, his disease resisting all medical treatment until a short time ago, when he was completely cured and restored to vigorous health by Dr. Williams' pick pills for pale people. " I have a wife and two children," he continued, " and when I was finally discharged as incurable I determined to make a fight for it. " For a time I lived with my parents at Warrington, where several medical men were consulted—with little advantages. Then I moved to Ashton-in-Makerfield, having obtained employment at the collieries of Richard Evans and Company, as an assistant electrician, and I could have done very well bad my health been gcod ; but I bad to give up, for, owing to the intense pains in my legs at night I could get no sleep, and loss of rest and pain made me unequal to the work of the day. I was in this extreme plight when the sudden ehange—ahnost miraculous—came over my prospects, 'and in less than six weeks I was working full time foe the Park Lane Colliery Company." ttind how did you cry you account for your changed fortune ? " asked the incredulous reporter. " I attribute it," repeated Mr Holden, "to the taking cf two boxes of Dr Williams' pink pillelfor pale people." " You are sure it wee Dr Williams' pink pills that did you this service ? " "I am Certain, hr I could not work until I started to take them six weeks ago. I found out as soon as I started the first box that they were doing me good, and if I had been abla to afford to buy a further supply when the second box was finished I should have been

thoroughly cured by now. As it is, I feel better than I I felt for eight years and lam cutting on flesh rapidly, whilat the pains have almost entirely gone from my legs." " How did yon name to bear of the value, af Dr Williams' pink pills for pale people ? Did someone recommend them ? " " Oh, no ! " replied Holden, "I read about what they bad done in the newspacers, and as everything else had failed,l thought I could but give them a trial.l wish now I had read about them years ago, but as it is it will be pPunds in mv pocket." *. But I suppose you do know of somebody else who has benefited by using Dr. Williams' pink pills ? " " Yes." he said, "there is a neighbour of owl, a woman (whom ha named; who had bornme reduced to a skeleton, but who is now quite healthy and fat in the face from taking them." " You don't mind my making use of the information you have given me ?" tasked the reporter. "No, certainly not ; " my wife and father and mother can tell you that I am speaking nothing hat what is true. The men at the Pit have also noticed the wonderful improvemet,t that has been effected in my ease, and they cannot help talking about it." "Ys." said Mr Holden. senior. who was standing by; "I had to take great care of him sixteen months after he came home, be was so ill, anri the great change this last six weeks has been remarkable."

- - The local recruits of the militia battaliona now on service in South Africa with some few detaila are being called up for preliminary drill. Those of the King's (Liverpool Iteßiment) have been ordered to assemble at Warrington. Warrington Conservatives at Liverpool.

The 14th annual conference and demonstration of the Lancashire and Cheshire Conservative Work- ing Men's Federation was held at Liverpool On Saturday. Warrington was represented by Coun— cillor Arthur Bennett, Mr William Holbrook (regis- tration agent), Mr Herbert Hayes (manager of the Junior Conservative Club), and others. In the morning on the invitation of Mr SW Higginbottora, M.P., the delegates were entertained to a trip on the river, when the steamship Violet, belonging to the Liverpool and Douglas line, conveyed the party down the river beyond the Formby Lightship. In • spite of the haze which hung over the river for a large portion of the time, the voyage proved 1 thoroughly pleasant. At a meeting in V:e evening Counsillor Bennett'support<rd a reeolution,submitted by Colonel Filkington, MP., approving of the 6 general policy of the Government. A Bit of irouble " with the Boers' 7 Mr J W Hayward, J.P. has received a letter from Private W Gregory, D Company let King's Liver- -1 pool Regiment, who is stationed at Waterval Onder _ Transvaal. In it the writer after desiring to be t remembered to his old friends at the Silver-stree t- Wealeyan School, briefly alludes to a " bit of trouble" his ,regiment had with the Boers, who were endeavouring to cross the line, and he says that he and other soldiers had to sit up for four nights in succession to prevent them doing so. He is in doubt whether his regiment will return home when the war is over, but two other battalions have been disbanded. He would like some time or other, to go out to India. He is disappointed at not being able to return to Warrington in time to witness the Walking Day.

div.head: LAMA =GISTS ILESEBTED. J
div.p: LAMA =GISTS ILESEBTED. J
AN OBSTINATE MAN,
Ey CLAI7DE TYERS.
PART IL

How difficult it is to predict in what manner cer- tain men will bear themselves in certain cir- cumstances. In the present case, of these three men, 'without doubt jovial Ben Wilson bekayed the most emotion, the least self-eoustraint at the dread. fed

. discovery. "God a' mercy! Tom Reynolds—head battered in—" he gasped,, then afterwards, "for mercy's sake, Short and Adams, if you can do without me going near it—touching it—say so. I could never abide the sight of blood since I was a child, any- thing else in the world except touching it," he en- treated, his whole body quivering. Also without doubt is it, that Mr. Short proved himself the calmest, the readiest of the three, for the

bluff simple farmer; between "profound agitation and natural rage at the deed, was almost at as great a standstill as his friend Ben. "There is not a moment to be lost," said Mr. Short energetically.. "The body is still warm to the touch, though I fear little hope for life. If you, Mr. Adams, run down to tho village for assistance and a stretcher, while I go back to watch for signs of life and try my brandy flask, we shall have done all in our power to save him. Wilson meanwhile had better drive off for the police; this vile crime has not been done much over half an hour, think of that, the man that did it may be quite close." So without further words Adams strode off for help ; Mr. Short returned to poor Tom Reynolds' al- ready stiffening clay; whilst Ben Wibton,.. whG
seemed to have lost the power of speech, 'lashed along the road to the nearest town, about four miles away, which I shall refer to as Sant,on. . . . .

Mr. Short found his vigil brief but trying. Setting aside the company of a murdered body, he began to speculate whether the assassin hiding in one of the numerous clumps of brushwood at this very minute, might not rush suddenly out to make yet another victim.
At last Farmer Adams came in sight with six or seven labourers and an improvised stretcher, the corpse was placed on, and they began their doleful march to the village. Little was said and then only
in whispers, but a solemn gloom overhung the party, such a gloom as can signify but one thing—the
presence a death. The farmer looked at his watch. "Can you be- lieve it, Mr. Short, it still wants a few minutes to one o'clock," he said. _ _ _ _ _
When they had passed almost clear of the lane, a sharp rustling in the hedge some distance ahead caused them, to a man to start nervously A tall
figure came slowly to meet them. " Why It's Bill Goose," said Farmer Adams '• I

had cleiin forgot that he ever lived much- less sending him to Watkin's, but he has brought the gun I see. Not much use for it to-day I'm afraid, Mr. Short. Come here, Bill, and bear a hand." . _ . . . .

Bill Goose took no n'otice 'of this order, his eyes, and through them what faculties he possessed, were iivetted on the burden the men carried, in spite of the two or three coats thrown over it, he seemed to

guess the secret. As they approached within a few yards he re- treated, keeping the same distance and without lift- ing his gaze in the slightest. "Why don't it walk ?" he gesticulated with out-stretched hand. No one hnswered him, and, turning suddenly, he fled with a ghastly "Ha, ha !" as if a hundred terrors pursued him. "Poor idiot," Murmured the farmer, "he may well be upset and bolt, I feel like it myself." "Bill be alway madder an' never when he see sommun dead," put in one of the labourers. "Ay," said another, "he'll go and run 'bout 'twixt the trees in the Wood, perhaps all night." Whether this was so or not no more was seen of _ _ _ _

Bill Goose that day, or little thought of him in truth, for Inspector Granger from Banton drove up with Ben Wilson very shortly. Inspector Granger was a highly reputed officer, very conscientious, almost to stubbornness indeed, in what he believed to be his duty, and perhaps a trifle narrow in judgment. He was well acquainted both with Mr. Short and Farmer Adams, intimate- ly so with Ben Wilson, who knew everyone in the county. " Glad yon'vecome. Granger, terrible affair this," said the farmer, thankful to think it was off iia shoulders now. "So it seems, but let us have a room to ourselves, and you and Mr. Short tell me all you know without delay. Poor Ben here is so cut up that I could get nothing really definite from him as we came along." "Ay, Ben is softer than a child in some things, I've always known," was the reply. They entered the house, and here Adams and Mr. Short between them related practically such an ac- count as is herein set down ; the Inspector made but one interruption, "Ben driving in his trap down Gipsies' Lane 1" he ejaculated, and added with a smile, "I suppose you said he couldn't, and then, of course, he must do it if he broke his neck at the trying." The farmer laughed himself: "You've hit it exactly, but he wouldn't drive back that way. But, merciful heavens ! it has just occurred to me that if Ben had persisted in the plan he said he wonlCancl had gone through the fields at that half-way dip, instead of the lane as 1 persuaded him, he might have passed within a courle of yards from where we found poor Tom Reynolds, and perhaps saved his life. We never know whether anything is for good or bad in this world," he concluded mournfully. "It is very doubtful if he would have noticed it, on account of the brambles, if the deed was actu- ally done then," Mr. Short opined. Their tale finished, Inspector Granger asked if the news had been broken to the wife and old mother of the dead man. • The family had not yet been told their loss. "You and I will go, Adams," said the Inspector decisively. He appeared rather a slow man in private life, but he was on duty now. "Mrs. Reynolds knows you 88 well as anyone, and I wish to get some information of her husband's recent movements if possible before she knows her loss. We shall come back by the place where you found hun, so that I can make a thorough examination." It was a great mistake if Inspector Granger im- agined that they could conceal or gloss over the stern actual facts of their tidings, until such moment as they thought fit to disclose them. Mrs. Reynolds was passing a front window when she heard the the farmer and Granger coming along the path to the house door, she stopped on the instant, and, turning her head, caught a glimpse of them. They drew near walking slowly, not to give grounds for suspicion, but she did not stir, not even that she might face them directly, but continued petrified, staring over her shoulder. When at length they entered the house she burst into a long wail: "He's dead, I know it, don't try to hide it, Tom's dead, I know," and she fell to sobbing and moaning before either had spoken a word. Presently the violence of her grief subsided, she sat down, and throwing her apron over head, listened in dumb misery. In the arm-chair by the hearth rested the old mother, her faculties failing under advanced age. At first not able to understand the whole grim truth, she tried to comfort the younger woman by saying, "Tom was sure to come back, sure to come back." Even at last when she did grasp the idea of death, old memories long since quieted but never erased, thronged to confnse her, and she muttered gently to herself of the death of her first son, dead before any present were born. "I told him many a time ue'er to go near the well, but he would go, he would go—" and so she kept on. Farmer Adams meanwhile stumbled through his tale, softening where he could best, though the wife never stirred under her apron or gave any signs of life. Suddenly old Mrs. Reynolds ceased her mumb- ling and sat straight up as if some word of the far- mer's had caught her ear. " Speak that again, Will Adams," she demanded. The farmer humoured her: "Mr. Short and me then went and told Ben Wilson on the other side of the lane," he repeated. The old woman rose from her chair like a sibyl and shrieked," It's that Ben Wilson done it. I tell ye that Ben Wilson done it." They tried to calm her but in vain, again and again she denounced him: Them Wilsons they hate us all like poison, it's him done it, I always said he would." When Inspector Granger had got what informa- tion he could, which amounted almost to nothing, they drove away, the last words ringing if:their efrs " It's that Ben Wilson done it." Although in the house they had both endeavoured to persuade the old woman that she was mistaken, that Ben Wilson of all people could never do such a thing, now as they sat side by side in the trap, a constrained silence reigned between them. Deny it or not, the unexpected denunciation of the aged woman had made a deep impression on their minds. The farmer puzzled himself pathetically but in vain to find words to express how preposterous, how ab- surd, such an idea was. He began to lose himself helplessly in the mass of circumstances ; he could not, disguiss it that his friend had been very near the place at the ye:7 time of the crin• . that his be.

Eaviour when they met was strange, the jesting words that had passed about his supposed tussle with Tom Reynolds loomed back to the farmer now in a most significant light. And then he thought of the notoriously bad terms that the men were on, and of their mutually fiery tempers, and his heart sank within him. An inopportune meeting, a few hot words, a first blow perhaps from Tom Reynolds, returned by his old friend with reckless fury—how . . .

easily such a tragedy might arise! Inspector Granger on his part made no attempt to open a conversation, but with a heavy gloom on his face sat weighing many small yet telling details. When they reached the nearest point by road avail- able to the gully, they left the old mare and trap and struck across the fields.

Here all at once a glimmer of light relieved tht farmer greatly, he broke out abruptly with, "At any rate, Granger, however awkward things may look, there's one thing can't be got over, Ben kept to the lane while Tom Reynolds, poor fellow, was in the field."

These were the first words spoken between them since they left Reynolds' house, but the Inspector understood without further explanation. "But Ben declared himself, you said, he would take to the fields at that gully," the Inspector com- mented.
"So he did when we were arranging it at home, then he changed his mind and kept to the lane, as I
advised."

"That's what he may have said to you," Granger replied curtly, but observing the dismay on Adam's face at this implied doubt,he asked, "Axe you sure that he did say so ?" "I think—l understood so, and hlr. Short," the farmer answered. _ _
All down the gully, except the bottom ditch where the water _drained, . the ground was _too dry to.pre-
, serve the indent of footmarks, nothing beyond the blood-dabbled tufts of grass boie evidence to the terrible crime. Still Granger ferretted about and at _

last gave vent to a low whistle. In the steep down- slope on the other side of the hollow from where the body hah lain, and at a distance of about five yards, were two small fresh slides or grooves in the ground. "Some stray beast must have slid down," the far- mer faltered. The Inspector gloomily shook his head with two words—" Iron shoes !"

He then led the way to the gate which opened into Gipsies' Lane, and there still in dumb show but without much surprise, as if his mind was already made up, pointed out to Adams the munistakeabla marks of wheels in the soft mud round the gateway, where a trap had entered the field from Gipsies

div.head: Lane.
div.p: Lane.

Farmer Adams, in his own none too critical dis- cernment, had anchored so much hope to the fact of Ben saying he had come by the lane all the way, while the murdered man lay in the field, that he was almost stunned at the uprooting of it thus. Still he made one more effort, "A man wanted a crowbar to give a blow the likes of that, now I know Ben hadn't nothing with him but a bit of a whip for the mare, and no timber was lying anywhere near the place' you know," he insisted. "Besides who could believe it of Ben ?"

_ "I can't believe it myself, but then in business of this kind I have to be a machine without beliefs or anything else, save keep my eyes open and act ac- cording,' responded the Inspector with genuine feeling. They walked back to the trap,- before taking their places, Granger examined the seat, cushions and rug; as he did so something rattled on the boards behind the seat. After a moment he drew to light a large murderous looking cudgel, evidently a stake pulled from the hedge; _ there were no marks on it save those of the soil. Neither of them said a word, but Adams' hope died away, while Inspector Granger's features grew yet darker and more stern. Kr. Short and Ben Wilson, who seemed to have somewhat recovered his spirits, were still alone in the same room, they looked up in surprise when, Granger and Adams entering, the former paused to lock the door after him. The officer of the law plunged into words without a moment's delay, like a man who saw an unpleasant task before him, and was determined to get through it at any cost. "Benjamin Wilson, I have now the most painful duty to perform I have had in my life, but duty is duty though it were my own brother. lam going to arrest you on suspicion of causing the death of Thomas Reynolds this day." The hay merchant sprang from his chair' his face blanched, his eyes dilated. " Merciful Father ! Arrest me for murder, you accuse me of murdering poor Tom Reynolds! You, an old friend, accuse me!" "No, Ben, I don't accuse you," the Inspector re- plied, evidently with emotion, " but it is my duty in this case to arrest any one against whom circum- stances point in a suspicious manner. If—and I trust to heaven it is so—you have had no hand in this crime, you have nothing to fear ' • you are not condemned, all the inquiry has to follow wheh the truth will be arrived at." It was Mr. Short who first broke silence : "If I might offer a suggestion," he said, " of course, In- spector Granger cannot allow anything to interfere with his duty, still he must have very strong ground for taking this course. Perhaps our friend 'Wilson, if he understood clearly what they were, might have some explanation which would rob them of their significance." ' All my doings have been as open as daylight, I can account for every moment," cried the hay mer- chant eagerly. Inspector Granger rubbed his brow as if to aid him to weigh the position up. "The main facts against you," he set forth slowly and carefully, "are these: first, the well-known bad feeling between you and the deceased, and the readiness you have shown on past occasions to come to actual blows : secondly, you were at the identical place within a few minutes of the doing of the crime, also it must be remem- bered driving over his own land, which he would probably object to ; thirdly, you were delayed an unreasonable time on ,the road, and your friends noticed, on seeing you at Red Ash, that you were agitated, your clothes being so suggestive of a struggle that Adams said in jest that you had been figiitng with Tom Reynolds." At this point Ben would have interrupted, but the Inspector held up his hand as a sign to let him finish. "Again," he continued, "you denied, or led them so to believe, that you had been through the fields at that gully, while as a matter of fact, you had.; and. last of all we find in your trap just such a heavy cudgel as might have struck the blow, though we know you hadn't it on startirtg. Bear in mind that these are not mere assumptions based on suspicious personal behaviour, but known facts; and it is my duty," he concluded, "to warn you that whatever you now say, may be used in evidence against you." The hay merchant stood aghast at this indictment. "How all this comes up against me I don't know, I can only tell you plainly and simply just what I did," he answered. "I left 'em as you know to go to Red Ash and managed to crawl down Gipsies' Lane as far as the first gate without hurt to myself or the trap. I determined to go by the fields across the gully as I knew there was nothing to fear in meeting Tom Reynolds, because we had seen each other since the time Adams knows of, and made it up again. That gateway is a very narrow one you may have noticed. I also found the gate would not stop open by itself, and as I could not hold it as well as guide the old Mrs through, there I was stuck three or four minutes for want of something to prop it open with, till I went back and pulled that stake out of the hedge It was easy enough then, and I was going to throw the stake away, when I remem- bered I might be in just such another pickle at the next gate, 80 I popped it into the trap instead. We were going as easy as you like, though the ground was steeper than I had thought, when, by that ditch, at the place where you saw the slides, the old mare threw up her head and eafiff4cl the air, twitch- ing her nostrils as if something disturbed her. if it had been in summer I should have said she had been stung by a horse-wasp. Not that I had time to think about it, for she lost her footing, her haunches slipped from under her, down she went and I rolled out of the trap before you could say 'knife!' I only felt dazed like at first, though I can tell you a man of my weight don't fall as light as a bit of thistle-down. I got the old mare on her feet, and then I found that both shafts were cracked, though you won't notice it unless you look closely. I was in a fme temper I can tell you ! This was why I was late meeting Adams and Short, and though I was beginning to feel sick and sore all over from the fall, I made up my mind not to tell 'em a word, be- cause Adams had said before starting I should do it, and,l didn't want everybody in the country crowing over me. When we met I let him think that I had taken his advice and kept to the lane, but it was mostly his own mistake. I was sulky enough too, I know, for I 'could scarcely sit up in the trap, my bones ached so' and I couldn't show it; so when the horror of poor Tom Reynolds came—well it finished me—there sno other word for it. That's my tale, gentlemen, 'cept perhaps this that Ben Wilson knows he has been a pig-headed fool many a time, but this is the pig-headedest 0f,a11." Inspector Granger paced to and fro weighing his old friend's explanations. A BID RECORD. —A middle-aged woman named Mary Bilgannon of no settled residence, was charved with steal- ing three pairs of stockings, of the value of Is 3d, from the shop of Messrs Corns, Cropper's-brow.—Superintendent Monaghan stated that the shop was in Butternaarket-street, and at five o'clock on the Ist April the prisoner was seen to take the stockings off a hook at the shop door, nut them Under her shawl and walk away with them. She suhse- quently offered them for sale et a second-isand clothes shop In Mersey-street, but did not succeed in disposing of them. The matter was reported to the police, and inquiries were made at a lodging-house on Friars'-green. where she had bees lodging, but it was 'Wend that she had disappeared. She was subsequently apprehended at Widnes and brought back to Warring !en by Sergeant Williamson. Prisoner was a travelling pedlar, and there was scarcely a tows in Lanca- shire and Cheshire in which she had not been convicted.— She was now committed to goal fir a month. COUNTY COURT BAILIFFS' DIFFICULTI/CS —KRIS WiICOONs, 11, Admiral-street, was summoned for having been drunk in Admiral-street, on the 28th May. She pleaded not guilty. —P.O. Howard said that be was sent to Admiral•street on Wednesday afternoon to see that no breach of the peace occurred whilst two County Court bailiffs were making a distraint. Defendant came out of her house drunk when be and the bailiffs passed along the street, and used ilthY and obscene language. There was a large crowd present. Defendant insisted on coming out after witness had put her in the house. She tried to incite the crowd to attack the bailiffs and witness.—Walter Newton, a County Court bailiff, stated that he went to Admiral-street on Wednesday along with William Burrevrs. They got the assistance of an officer, to prevent any !breach of the peace. He Saw the woman come out and use disgusting language —William Burrows another bailiff corroborated and said time defendant shoute I " That man (Newton) ought to have been shot when he was at the front."—P C Hayes also gave evidence.—Three witnesses were called by the defend- ant and stated that she did not leave her doorstep. It was alleged that the constable threw her into the house.—The Chief Constable said that this case was a sample of what officers had to do in a district like that. Not only were they harraseed, but when the cases came into Court, an attempt was made to out-swear them,—A. fine of be and costs was Inflicted, amounting in all to £l. AN ABUSIVL TRAMP.-11fary Fletley, who described her- self as a tramp, was charged with begging in Bridge-street on Saturday.--P.O Bratt proved the offence and described the prisoner as one of the worst characters he ever had to deal with.—She kicked the superintendent's wife most violently.—On promising to leave the town the prisoner wan discharged. A Ulu rum or IN TROUBLE—Dominic Toole, of no fixed residence, was charged with being drunk and disorderly at 8 p.m., on Saturday night.—P C. Davies stated that the prisoner was drunk and was creating a great disturbance by kicking a woman with whom he was in company. Prisoner said he had come home from South Africa twelve months ago. He had beea on active service with the Bast Lancashire Regiment. lie had there had two severe illnesses, and since then a glass of anything got into his head. He was very sorry and would leave town if the bench would let him off.— Di s charged . BEGGING.—JaMes Bowyer. a tramp, was Charged with begging.—P.C. The "Times " states that the current of feeling in Ministerial circles is running strongly in favour of making the cost of education an Imperial rather than a local charge, and the belief is confidently expressed that the Cabinet will be found prepared to meet their wishes of their supporters in this matter. The Bing has ordered that the ancient Royal barge which in modern days has been a picturesque object on the great lake at Virginia Water is to be put in thorough order at Staines. It was built in 1689, the first year of the reign of William and Mary, and its times of British oak are still in a good state of preservation. The "trim- bunt wherry " has the high stern of the period, bearing mspicuously the Royal Arms,and there are thwarts for ten rowers. One of Its most striking features is an elaborate minopy.

PEACE I THERE is one word which has been hr every- one's mouth during the last few days wherever men have talked itogether of the coming of

peace. The word is neither 2: THE NATION'S triumph nor exultation—it is simply " relief." The long nightmare is over. We have ended the organised effort to spill the blood of men whom we heartily admired even for the very obstinacy which protracted the war. There is an end to the suspense of those who had friends or kinsmen daily exposed not merely to shot and shell, but to privation and disease. Nor are our soldiers and our new fellow-citizens the only gainers. Peace releases us from the nightmare which had disorganised our national life, thrown the wheels of civil- isation out of gear, burdened „our resources, I aggravated the poverty of the poor, and threaten- ed us all with a reaction whichlhas not spared even the most stable traditions of our national life. All that has come to an end. Our soldiers are free, and their laurels await them. The country seems ready to welcome the B3et- to' citizenship and friendship. It lies now with our manhood to combat the reaction at home which owed its temporary success solely to the war. For the rest, it is our duty to hope. The pacification of South Africa, the resettlement of a devastated desert, the healing of the scars made by the burn- ing of homesteads and the mismanagement of the OCamps," will be no light task. But at:least we have made a beginning. It is vain now to regret a war which need never have come about, and useless to protest against an annexation which might have been avoided. The country is in kindly and gener- ous temper, and that is the best omen for the future. On the morrow:of peace the" Standard" vied with the " Morning,Leader " in its eulogy of our:gallant and patriotic foes; and the splendid testimonial which Sir HENRY CAMPBELL-BANNBR- MAN gave totheir "military qualities,their tenacity of purpose, their self-sacrificing devotion to liberty and country" drew cheers from both sides of the House. While that spirit lasts, if it informs not only the country at home .but the officials on the spot, there is hope of an enduring peace and a real reconciliation.
RELIEF.

THE terms of peace have been drafted in a care- ful document drawn with considerable skill by lawyers from both sides. It is the work not only of Lord MILNER and Sir THE:TERM3 RICHARD SOLOMON, but Of OF PEACE. Judge HERTZOG and ex-Attor-

ney-General SMUTS. It is a real treaty, as different from the "unconditional surrender" which Lord ROBERTS demanded in 1900 as could well be imagined. It is also very much more generous in its details than the KITCHENER-BOTHA terms of 1901. It begins by according the fullest amnesty to all the burghers of both Republics. The fatuous banishment pro- clamation of last ,Septem)er is "tacitly !dropped," to use Lord MILNER'S phrase. Every burgher or prisoner who accepts the document and acknow- ledges his position as a subject of King EDWARD is assured in the possession of his "personal liberty and property." He may retain his rifle where his safety in a lonely district requires it. The Dutch language is not to b 3 proscribed. It is a pity,perhaps,that it is not at once accorded the status which it enjoys :in Cape Colony—an alternative official language, like French in Lower Canada, on an equality wit'a English—but as it is to be allowed in schools and courts of justice no real harm is done. It is when we reach the finan- cial provisione;that the greater generosity of these terms, as compared with Mr CnixthaaLAlN's in 1901, is most apparent. He had declared that those"offers would " never be repeated." its point of fact,they were not only repeated but improved. He then characterised as " preposterous " Lord KITCHENER'S suggestion that free grants should be made to re-settle the burghers who had lost their all in the war. Ad yet, after all, free grants are to he made to all "who owing to war losses are unable to prov;de. themselves with food, shelter, and the necessary amount of se )cl, stock, implements, &C." Then he VVSS willing to s(4 apart £1,033,030 to in set the tio'lt contract:od by the late Republics to their burghers. To-day a 5 much as £3,090,000 will be given freely. In addi- ion to this sum, there:is provision for loans to an indefinite extent to individual burghers, which will be free of interest for two years, and there-
,C
I

after will be burdened only with 3 per cent, on easy terms of repayment. In short, as )fr. LLOYD. GEORGE neatly puts it, our opponent has lost • his case, but we pay his costs on the higher -scale. Better still, the working of this scheme of resettlement is to be left to local representa- tive committees. If only we have the wisdom to allow these bodies to express their minds freely on all local question which arise from time to time, there is here from the very start a boginning of self-governing. A wise Governor will gradually expand these bodies into County Councils. Finally, there is a clause which promises ultimate self-governmeut " as soon as 2ircumstances permit." It is a vague phrase, which leaves everything to our sense of honour and our instincts of statesmanship. If, as Lord SALISBURY foreshadowed, we delay the fulfilment of this promise—" it may be for years, it may he for generations "—then this peace can be only a brief respite from strife, a mere intermission of war. If, on the other hand, we realise that nothing can pacify South Africa or relies e us of the burden of an armed peace short of the full grant of autonomy, then we shall hasten to take the first step towards it as soon as the Boers have been re-settled and the industry of the country re- started.

The great flaw of this treaty of pe ice is that it makes no provision for the Cape rebels who joined the Boers, not so much from a platonic sympathy, as from despera- THE CASE OP THE tion caused by the abuses of Martial Law. The provi- sion f:or their future is con- tained, not in the treaty itself, but in a note drafted by the Cape Government. Apparently— though this is far from clear —those rebels who elect to remain in the late Republican territory will escape pains and penalties. But a intictk harder fate awaits those who surrender in the C )lony itself—a fate So hard that one doubts whether they will be in any hurry to surrender. The rank-and-file, to be sure, will escape with disfranchisement for life. Toe leaders, however, are to be tried by the local tribunals, and on them any penalty short of death may be indicted. rats is not the generous amnesty which public opinion in this country had demanded. There is small ',hope of pacification if some Judge JEFFREYS is to be sent out on a Bloody Assize, while every eft orb ought to be made to forget the war and he ii the racial strife.So me period of disfranchisement is possibly a just penalty; but to create a large class of lifelon g helots—hrin ired of thorn were lads who ware driven
REBELS.

. - Into rebellion by every conceivable provocation is the maddest thought that ever eatered into the head of a states:lan. If the constitution of Cape Colony is to Los suspended, and a Class of voteless and hopeless mislcontents created, we shalt undo in Cape Colony all the good which our relative goner- Osity might accomplish north of the Orange River. The two problems canno'.; be separated. The Bears Will sympathise with their southern kinsmen, and -sooner or later a day of reckoning will Come. But , let us hope that the KING will see his way, as an 'act of grace, to issue a generous pardon to these rebels who are at present outside the amnesty Which the burghers have obtained. 9

The report of the Warrington auditors for the Year ended 31st March has been issued. Of recent Years these reports have attracted special atten- tion from an observant public, and the one issued this week fully maintains the standard of interest. There is one paragraph of considerable significance. We quote it, as follows "Business is frequently done with Limited Companies of which members of the Corpor- ation are shareholders; in connection with sundry payments it was necessary to inspect contracts relating thereto ; we have also in- spected the competitive tenders, and in the few instances where the accepted tender was not the lowest of those received, have made further inquiry. In each such case we have received explanations which have satisfied us :that the selection has been made for the public good, and in the interests of the ratepayers." 'careful consideration of this clause in the report leads to one or two conclusions. First, it is obvious that the auditors, and particu- larly one of them, have not been unmindful of the circumstances in which they were elected. It will be remembered that Mr. Bradshaw headed the poll as the nominee of the Municipal Non- Trading Association. Some pronouncement on the vexed question of "municipal trading," or certain aspects of it, was therefore expected when the report came to be published. That anticipa- tion has not been falsified, for the paragraph we 'quote makes unmistakable allusion to trading between the Corporation and limited companies Possessing members of the Corporation as share- holders. And this is what has come to be known as "municipal trading "—as "immoral trading." -But the auditors, independent men with a full knowledge of what is expected of them, de not dis- approve of this kind of trading, nor even the accepting of a tender not the lowest of those sub- nutted. They have taken each case on its merits and looked at if from :the viewpoint of men appointed to safeguard the welfare of the public \ and they say "we have received explanations ' which have satisfied us that the selection has been made for the public good, add in the interests of the ratepayers.' An opinion could not be more unmistakably expressed and it goes to confirm the belief increasingly held that while "municipal trading" can and may be immoral, it is not all immoral, and there is oven less of it immoral than we have been led to believe. MATTERS OF MOMENT. A ProvjTa Letter. Peace, weleome and glorious, at last ! Althonet the joyful news was not issued from the War Office Anti' five p.m on Sunday,it had reached many of the Most distant and out-ot-the-way places in the pro- inces in:time for an announcement tobemad bete e to congreeations at all the churches and chapels the conclusion of the respective services. And the fl.rst day of the week,which was also the first of the Ica, °nth, with all the hallo Wed associations, that laave clung to it thiough the centuries, has seldom been used to happier and more appropriate purpose 4tian when, on this "glorious let ot June," there as annouticed to all the people throughout the the glad tidings of Peace. A. Correspondent, 037 the way, directs attention to ano! her great let Of June announcement, and to the fact that S g un- 'ay last wee the anniversary of Lord Howe's victory oVer the French. The twenty-seven sail of 1,15 line battleships were defeated by twenty-five -anglish warships at Cape St Vincent. He thinks ,hat June Ist will, in future, be beet known as the nate on which peace between the British and the '(1)10ers was announced throughout England in 1902. f course' the celebrations of the peace declaration have differed widely in this and other countries, 4cCording to the point of view. But in the English Drovincee, generally speaking, flags, trumpets, and Processions were much in evidence, and thanks- RlVing services have been held in the various places 2t worship, attended by the leading ecclesiastic "a civic dignitaries, and ;large congregations of a really thankful people.

'The Coronation Festivitieslhave certainly not been t°B ight of. Indeed, the display of bunting is said ° heoze been limited in many instances during the aSt Week in anticipation of the demand that will 8 Made for the coming 26th and 27th. While in- apace has been received iu this country that

!the two days mentioned have been proclaimed as public holidaysat Prstoria,the Coronation holidays sofa as toe whole of the provinces are concerned, cannot yet be said to have been definitely settled. The London Board School children are to be released from wok a full week, dating from the 23rd, so tim they may be free to participate in all the public jubilations incidental to the occasion. A letter was issued from the Vrivy Claacit Office a week ago, to the effect that the King had then wider consideration the suggestion that all children attending school in the provinces should in like manner be granted the full week's holiday. His Majesty's wishes in such a matter constitute a command, and there should, of course, be an im- mediate response to the Royal desire that all the schools in the country should be closed during Coronation week, It is both desirable and neces- • sary to adequately impress the mind of the young with the significance of the hiAoric occasion, and few devices are better calculated to do this than the luxury of a whole week's holiday at this de- lightful period of the year.

it has ben observed that there is " nothing rare " ab mt the new sovereigns that have been except their presence in the average pocket. What is meant is that there is no value beyond twenty shillings in each coin. Some people have treasured the gold because they imagiuPd it had a mistake upon it in the spelling of the King's name. The supposed " W," if examined closely, will be found to be a double "U," which puts the Latin right. The " U," of course, was originally always written " V " in Latin, and is still so written in much of the ornamental lettering done for eccle- siasticali'and other purposes.

Writers on agricultural topics who seek to bring the farmer abreast with the times, have for some weeks past been harping upon the possible advent of Motor Ploughs, and time alone appears to be needed to bring into the field what has hitherto constituted but a standing joke. Mr Edison, who 'is reported to have recently said that " electric vehicles for city work, delivery waggons, etc., will soon supersede all other kinds of vehicles," has keptyhis word too well for the world seriously to , doubt that what he says of the capabilities of his ne storage battery is true, and the expectations of its effsctslwell founded. The new battery seems calculated to work quite a revolution, not only in ' street traffic: but in a number of different ways. For, if a motor wheel can be made to revolve for a journey of a hundred miles without the:battery which drives it being re-charged, there are infinite varieties of work to which a battery so marvellously constructed can be adapted. It may be said to not only suggest the motor plough of the future, but at the same time:to warn horses off the highways and by-waysAwholesale.The question may well be asked already whether the railway is to be revolutionised and the ocean steamer is to be re-named because of steam being no longer necessary. He would indeed be a bold man who should pretend to set limits to what may be accomplished, and that ere many years—or perhaps months—elapse, by an agency so powerful, so adaptable, and yet so easily controlled.

It may surprise some people t 3 be told that the two leading fishing ports ot Grimsby aod Hull have a capital of at least four and a quarter miilions invested in Steam Trawlers, while the total value of the fish landed in the United King- dom in one year, taken at 11c1 a pound, was £9,688,000. A supply of food such as this, close at hand, to a cuuntry largely dependent on outside sources for the means of exi,,tenco, can scarcely be over-estimated. An average year's catch would thus by a comparison of weight, be equal to a flock of 10,263,220 sheep, and 1,047,267 cattle. The sailors lead a hard life, certainly ; but they are all well louder discipline, and have their own " admirals," whose commands they are bound to obey. There is reported to be a large proportion of teetotalers among them, of whom ,the: Rechabites furnish a considerable, contingent.

One is reminded here of a fear that is expresled in some of the repots presented by " the trade " that Mr Ritchie's Licensing Bill will prove extremely harrassing to that body if passed as it now stands, while in other reports it is acknowledged that the Bill has some good points. It has long ' been considered a grievance that notwithstanding a reduction of licences for consumption on the pre- rnagis trates have not the power to refuse applications for new grocers' licences. This, of course, will be altered under the Bill, and it is hoped that a spirit of intelligent discernment will be brought to bear upon clubs, so that the publican may not be prejudiced by rival institutions con- ducted under fewer restraints, and with possibly a greater power of evil. The sale of drink is a vast and embarrassing subject, and no doubt much un- reasoning prejudice has been imported into it along with the efforts of conscientious and fair-minded men to place it upon a better footing.

It was fitting, perhaps, that the first rAy.r.>e which the Australian Cricketsrs experienced in England should hare been received this week at the hands of the splendid Yorkshire team. There:is no county team which it is more agreeable to con- gratulate, except our own, of course, than that of the keen and honoarable sportsmen who represent Yorkshire. The Lustralians certainly had some hard luck, notably, no doubt, in the enforced absence of frumble on a bowler's wicket. They struggled hard for victory, but their bowlers,clever though they are, were not quite so deadly as Hirst and Mr Jacksm on a treacherous pitch. It is worthy of note that the dismissal of the Australians was accompanied by these bowlers without there being any need to call on Rhodes, who bowled so wonderfully at Birmingham. The manager for the Australians must now regret the candour with which he de- clared a few weeks since that the Australians did not think much of Rhodes and Hirst, but perhaps they do not just now care to think of them at all, the subject being a little too painful.

The National Association4of.! Master Bakers and Confectioners has this week been holding its fifteenth annual conference at Bristol, the procee l- ings being opened by the Lord Mayor of the City on Tuesday. The report presented to the Conference, in allusion to the subject of Underground Bake- houses, said there could be no question that the cry for the abolition of such conditions was popu- lar, but that " like most popular opinions it is largely founded upon fallacious ideas and ignorance of the subject." To which it might be replied, perhaps, that fallacious and ignorant as popular opinions may be" mostly" they practically govern the country,by selecting and determining who shall be its representatives,and will in the end also have an important bearing upon the settlement of the underground bakery question. In the meantime the" Daily News," dealing with underground work- rooms generally,expresses the hope that Mr Ritchie is not going to wait until Germany has abolished such places before he dexides to "regulate and in- spect these horrible places out of existence." To have them at all is certainly bad enough, but to have our bread baked in and supplied from them will probably not much longer be tolerated.

div.head: WIDNES F.C. -A SUCCESSFUL SEASON.
div.p: WIDNES F.C. -A SUCCESSFUL SEASON.

The batance-sheet for the past season of the Widnes Football Club has been issued this week. it is an interesting document, and shows that though the club started the season with an adverse or debit ' balance of £342 63 id, this has been reduced by a substantial remaining balance of £133. The receipts totalled .C 1,301 12s, and comprised the following items :—First and secml team gate money, £485 17s 6d ; North,,rn Union and South- West Lancashire Cup Competitions, £258 3s 9d; training tickets, foot races, and transfers, £33 7s 6cl; -vorks and schoolboy competitions' gate money, £B2 9s3d ; Widnes Athletic Club, £55 ; members subscriptions and donations, £93 lie 61 ; proceeds Christmas draw, concert, and ball, £B3 2s 2d. On the other side, wages, £303 2e 61 ; and railway and hotel expenses, £143 17s Sc], were the most con- siderable items. Th,. annual meeting will be held next week. NARROW ESCAPE FROM DROWNING AT RUNCORN On Sunday evening, just about the time that the news of the conclusion of peace had been received at Runcorn, two girls named Sarah and Mary Gilli- gan, aged respectively seven and five years, were walking along the towing path of the Bridgewater Canal at Top Locke, when they fell into the water. , They were in imminent peril of drowning when 'Edward liampson, of 19, Crescont-row, promptly rushed to the rescue. By the aid of a boat hook he succeeded in reaching one of the children, and as he was lifting her out of the water he discovered her little sister clinging tightly to her foot. Both were at length brought en to the bank, and con- veyed to their home in Fryer-street, where they soon recovered from the effects of their immersion Ilampson deserves to be commended for his prompt- ness. Iteeems that the children were anxious to see the placard containing the peace news, and find- lag their way blocked by the large crowd on Savage's Bridge they went round by the back of the old crate warehouse in the hops that they might achieve their object if they reached the bridge from the steps leading to the towing path. The Runcorn Forward" Lodge 2444, held its lid session in the Ashrid ge-street Mission on Monday evening last, and a good muster of members put in an appearance which is a very hopeful indication, con9idering the great attractions in the town con- cerning the proclamation of peace. Bro Ander took the chair at 730 and opened the session according to the ritual. The following are the elected officers: C P and L D, Bro Anders; V P, Sister Anders; Sec, E H Hildidge ; TreaQ, Bro J Soyle ; Chaplain' Bro Midge; Fin Sec, Sister A Hayes; Guard, Sister Woodier: P C P Sister R03C09 ; Marshall, Bo Hayes. The Chairman stated that a hopeful future was before the Lodge, providing aggressive efbrts were male. Bro Francis of St Helens Seliveed the charter of the Lodge, and spoke of the general ad- vantages of the Order. Bro Patrick presented the Lodge with a set of regalia and gavel, being a most valuable gat. The No 1 Convention, South-We ,t Lancashire, was invited to hold its July session in Runcorn, when a further impetus will be given to the new Lodge. During the evening one new mem- ber was made and several other persons were proposed.

Last Friday afternoon Mr J C Cragg, senior assistant, who has been appointed head ,master of the Froisham Endowed t•ichool,was presented with a handsome stationery cabinet as a token of the esteem in which he is held by the teachers and scholars. The head master Mr J F Moulton in making the presentation referred in complimentary terms to Mr Cragg's long connection with the school, and to the great success which had attended his efforts, He had performed all hss work in the most faithful and efficient manner possible. On be- half of the teachers and scholars he wished him every success in his new sphere of labour. (Ap- plause.) Mr Cragg who was loudly cheered thanked them all cordially for the handsome gift, and spoke of the friendly relations which had always existed between Mr Moulton and himself and all the mem- bers of the staff He would continue to take an interest in the school although he was leaving, and would be pleased at all times to hear of its con- tinued succesQ. (Applause). Before dispersing the scholars gave three hearty cheers for Mr Cragg,and the singing of "For he's a jolly good fellow," brough;, an interesting ceremony to a close.

div.head: D7ATH OF MR. RICHARD WALTON, NEWTON.
div.p: D7ATH OF MR. RICHARD WALTON, NEWTON.

Many of our readers will regret to hear of the sudden death of Mr Richard Walton, glass manu- facturer, of Crow-lane, Newton-le-Willows, which took place on Sunday morning at the age of 63 years, Mr Walton had been in failing health for a short time past, and on Saturday night whilst in bed was seized with an apoplectic fit. On Sunday morning he was discovered in bed unconscious. Medical aid was summoned,but recovery was hope- less and the deceased gentleman passed away peacefully. The deceasen was a Conservative in politics and an ardent churchman being a regular attendant at the Wargrave Church. In charitable matters he was very open handed, and his presence in the district will be greatly missed. He took the greatest interest in the progress of trie war, and it was unfortunate that his end should come before he was aware of the Conclusion of peace. The funeral took place on Wednesday afternoon, the interment being in the Wargrave Churchyard. The principal :mourners were Mr G Walton and Mr S Walton (brothers), Mrs McCruge and Mrs Mullinder (sisters), Miss Hughes, Mr J G Walton (nephew), Mrs John Walton, Mr C B F Borron, and Mr Thomas Molyneux. A large number of the workpeople followed the funeral corteff e, and half a dozen of the workmen acted as carriers.

The coffin was of -panelled oak with heavy brass fittings but at the express wish, of the deceased, there were no flowers' Tha funeral service was carried out by the Rev J. Carson, and the whole arrangements were undertaken by Messrs Waitcn and Son.
