div.head: EXAMINER FRIDAY JUNE 6, 1902
div.p: THE EXAMINER FRIDAY JUNE 6, 1902
RUNCORN NOTES.

[BY TRIBUNIISI. This month tne "Parish Magazine " waxes amusingly pathetic. Its adherents may think it justly states in fair, set terms a crying scandal of , the times, but outsiders, generally, will read the effusion with feelings more akin to merriment,than ' sympathy for the writer. After carefully noting the fact (?) that "Nonconformist ministers have asked tor places during the Coronation , service in the Abbey " the article continues to deplore that anyone should have thought the " festivities " a good opportunity for undoing the compromises of the past by " scoring victories over the Church of England in the town. On a national occasional it was reasonable enough that the National Church should in a school procession be recognind by the poqition allotted to its oldest Sunday school, but the fighting spirit would have its own way by no means to the promotion of godly union and concord, and it is left to us ooor chui•ch people to do the best Toe can under the circumstances,"

The quotation proves that Canon Wood believ.is a great amount of injustice has been done to the Establishmeut by the civic authorities. Far from falling in as an amicable"minority with the vote of the town the rev gentleman's party still urge the paramount claims of the Church in leading the van on the historic day although they know the order of procession has been fairly and definitely decided by ballot. Really one would think for the sake of "godly union and concord," if for nothing else, the whole controversy might be allowed to sink into ob'ivion. The sooner men recognise that clericalism is not to be allowed to push its claims unduly the sooner will concord and harmony reign Once more in this whilom Marry Runcorn of ours. The clerical party is not yet the predominant power it wishes to be The; Vox Fo,ona is dead against the usurpation. And when " Vox and Pop " are combined no amount of clerical influence can possibly win the game no matter how they appear, for a time, to be sweeping in the stakes.

It is complained that the civic authorities in fixing the time of the priNcession have left the pro- ceedings of the Establishment altogether outside their calculations. And, somewhat unreasonably,it is urged that the processioo, inclusive of the public bodies, the clubs, the friendly societies, &c., &c., should have meekly waited with folded hands until the service at the Parish Caurch had finished, and made their arrangements accordingly. With all due respect to the holders of such a presumptuous idea it can justly be urged that while they and their views I represent but a single sect, the arrangements already organized carry with tnem imprimatur of tha entire town. Mr Taylor in this matter is the representative of 20,000 people, who all respect his firmness and judgment.

Far different is the attitude "of Father Chambers and the I\bnconformist ministers. Animated by the truest feelings of loyalty, patriotism,and amity, they have sacrifi?.ed tneir own wishes in order to join in with the general demonstration of thanks- giving which one expects from a united populace oa such an occasion.

Tearfully enough the Vicar says " It is left to us poor church people to do the best we can under the circumstances." Just imagine the false position conjured up by such a phrase. The strongest cleric in the town—ana one who wields an enormous power—describing the representatives of a church the most highly favoured in the land, as" poor j churchmen." The Vicar is undoubtedly sincere, and the church may be poor in the sense that it cannot get all its own way at certain times,but the phrase ,is none the less intentionally misleading. Any outsider roe ling this lugubrious sentence would ' naturally suppose that the Church party were the victims of 8311:10 dire conspiracy combining to sap the foundation of the Anglican Church and bring it to the ground. But the average Run;:orniaa knows perfectly well that the sentence quoted is the direct result of a direct refusal of a town'o meeting to allow clericathm ta dominate the will of the people.

The worthy Vicar would do well to notice the attitude of his erstwhile henchman the Vicar of Over. There, the Ray W LI Staoles has most , cordially agreed to the ballot, and, I believe, has actually postponed for a short time his service in order tc contribute to the goneral harmony of the arrangements. It is also to be feared that should the Canon seek for pity on the other side of the river, his fellow Churchmen would only lecture him for his narrow intaler.ince, For be it knopra that in Widnes—where the Churchmen are in an overwhelming majority—they have graciously agreed to tha ballot which so distresses the Vicar of Run Corn.

I would strongly counsel the Canon to slightly defer the hour of sErvica at the Parish Church in order that all shades and sections ofthe community may be represented. Such a concession would be the first step towards making the embittered Run- corn of b-day into the happy Runcorn of Canon Barclay's days. The Nonconformist section would thus see that toleration was not an unknown word in the Anglican Church, and a fuller recognition of each other's position would be the happy and inevitable result.

[By A CORRESPONDENT.] It is worthy of note that the Runcorn District Council and the Runcorn Urban Council have both virtually pronounced against the Education Bill. At present, feeling runs very strong in Runcorn that the bill should be either mended or ended— preferably the latter. So far 119 further steps have been taken to oppose the bill but at the public meeting held some time ago under the auspices of the Free Church Council feeling was unanimous against it,

The prisoners at the Runcorn Police Court on Monday Were among those who substantially felt the good effects of the peace, The Chairman, Mr F J Norman, after a concise and happy:speech com- memorative of the event, let the majority of the prisoners eff with very light sentences, which seemed to be very much appreciated.

Mr Imison's speech convinced the . majority present that the committee had acted wisely in refusing to spent more money than the £6OO in the scheme. It will be a blessing to the town it the streets ever become congested in the way it is anticipated. But in spite of sanguine hopes the Bridge will have to do an enormous traffic—which it has not yet been proved by anyone that it can do—baforo such a happy consummation will be reached

div.head: Warrington Man Killed at Widnes. . .
div.p: A Warrington Man Killed at Widnes. . .

.11r Brighou-se conducted an inquiry az, the Coroner's Court, Warrington on Thursday evening, into the circumstances attending the death of Timothy Costello, who died at the Warrington Infirmary on Wednesday from injuries sas- tained by a fall at Messrs Gossaga's- works at Widnes. lit W J Porshatv appeared on behalf of the contractor, Mr Peter Rigby, of Warrington. —The evidence of the deceased's daughter,Margaret .Ward, was to the effect that her fatrier WM a bricksetrers' labourer, liviag at 37, Ohl-road, Latchford, and was 60 years of age. lie wai brought home on Saturday, suf- feringfrorn injuries, and was attended to by Dr. Langdale. lie was ultimately removed to the In- firmary where he died on Wednesday.—ftdward Evans, bricksetters' labourer, of 15, Lord Nelson- street, stated that be, deceased and other workmen were employed by Mr Peter Rigby in erecting a large chimney at Messrs Go3sage's works, Widnes. On Saturday morning, deceased was walking across a plank when he missed his footing and fell a distance of of Oft. 61n.—By Mr Forstaw : Deceased was the foreman labourer, and erected the plank in question. It was 2ft. wide and had been used for a fortnight by the workmen.- -Mr Rigby gave it as his opinion that the deceased had been startled by someone calling to him from the top of the chimney and had missed his footing. —Nurse Garnett said the deceased was admitted to the infirmary on Monday morning. He was suffer- ing from fractured ribs and died on the following Wednesday morning.—The jury returned a verdict of " Accidental Death," and added that no blame wag attached to anybody.

THE APPROACHES TO THE WIDNES AND RUNCORN BRIDGE. The Highways and Building Committee reported teat the following letter ha ben received re the Widnes and Runcorn Bridge from Mr John Webster the engineer under date 7th May:—" I attended the meeting of the directors yesterday, and the questdm er the Belvedere- road WAS discueeed,and I am sorry to say it was decided hot to proceed with the road as proposed, but simply to construct the approach as required by the Act. lam sorry your Council have acted ID unreasonably in the matter, after having been met, I consider, so hand- somely by the Bridge Company and the Ship Canal Cunpamy. Tuey must also remember that they are large shareholders in the company, and we cannot ex- pect the scheme to pay if we are to be loaded with the , costl of works which really do not form part of the scheme. I have received Me Hunter's final reply, and he will not Sanction the elope ; firstly. because ititakes up considerably more land than they had offered,: and secondly, because by setting back his rails, it makes the gradient of the approach to the wharf about 1 in 16, which is certainly too great for taeavy traffie. I think it will be very advisable for you to get the land con- veyed from the Ship Canal Company, as soon as possible otherwise it may be tho late." Mr I °met moved the adoption of the minute'. He said that with reference to the lettee received b r the Council, they had not given the matter the consideration they ought to have done. The C nmeil had been prema- ture in closing the question. Toe Belvedere approach was the only piece of land that the Manchester Ship Canal Company had in their district unoccu- pied, and in which they, as a town were interested. When the Snip Canal cho,e to expand it would be at that p trticular point and therefore their prosperity as a town was ound up to a certain extent in that quarter of the town. roe Cauaell should in the first place have replied to the effect that at present they were not prepared to spend more bat were prepared to reconsider their decision at a future dattaif circum- stances warranted it. As it was they had closed the matter by limiting their offer to £6OO. So eatisfied were the Bridge Company with the anticipated prosper- ity of the bridge that they were themselves going to spend £1,600. The district should certainly be opened up and it was advisable that the tows should have an interest in the matter. Mr Wilson seconded.

_ Mr Imisoa pointed out that the closure was applied by the Bridge Co.. and not by the Council. The com- mittee were willing to contribute a certain sum but no more as the cost was an uncertain one. The people most likely to gain frem the new approach would be the Bridge Company and the Ship Canal Company. The object of the road was to prevent supposed congestion which might exist in the centre of the town. A great many people preferred that the congestion would make itself felt and hoped that the Council would not give £5OO until it had become acute. Traffic would thus have to go up the leading thoroughfares and tradesmen cni4ht possibly benefit. lie had had it on good authority that if they hal spent the money a town's meeting would have been called and their action as a Council would have been probably condemned. He considered that they had proposal to spend a reasonable surn especially as their share capitai was only 10 per cent. In Widnes they were rict spending moley in approaches and if they were it would have modified his views. Mr Bisbrown agreed with Mr Imison. 'racy were forced to come to a decision owing to the Bridge Com- pany asking for a definite answer. They offered £6OO out of a total of £1,040 yet that was not deemed suffi- cient.

Wiswall deprecated Mr Webster in his letter term- ing the action of the Connell as unreasons.ble. He thought some action on,ght to ba tak3o on the matter. It was purely a matter of finance which privent3.l the town from contributing more than the sum named and was altogether a serious matter for the town.

Buckley-street P.S.A. Open Meeting.

The monthly open meeting of this society was held To the Methodist Free Church, B decoy-street Sundav afternoon, and was presided over by Mr W Wright. Mr James Ball was the speaker. Mrs J Hannan rendered eff )ctive:y " Behold, I stand at the door," and Mr J Hann so was Fq sally aporaciate l in the rendition of " A dream of Hope," and " Star of Bethlehem." Mr Albert Trow was the accompanist. The Chairman said th P.S A. had berm the means of attracting many young men, and had led them to be a blessing to many. Although, perhaps, the movement had not done all the good its promoters thought it would do, nevertheless ir had accomplished much good work—it had given life land energy to all connected wit's the 'churches. He did not kn ow of anything which would help to make men better so mach as association with a P.S.A.—Mr James Ball, in the course of an address thought that if they had one desire more than another, it was the desire to be happy. He did not think that God had implanted that desire within their hearts to be a trouble to them but that it might be continually satisfied ; but the methods whereby the satisfaction was derived should be carafully selected and prayerfully acted upon. They must not 1 ook to passing things, which were practically worthless, • for their guidance but to God.
Bold-street Wesleyan Church.
Sunday School Anniversary Services

The annicnraary services in connection with Bold- street Wesleyan Sunday School took place on Sunday. when sermons were preached by the Rev Robert Colley, of London, who folds the important position of secre- tary to the VV esleyan Suniay School Union. The morning service was well attended. when Mr Culley spoke from the words "The life that now is." The special hymns were sung by the children in a very pleasing manner, and the anthem "Jean, Priceless Treasure" (J V Roberts), was admirably rendered by the choir. Mr g A Booth and Mr Hassall rendered the solo items. Mis B icith also sang " The Voice of the Father " (Cowen) in a manner which heartily pleased the congregation. In the afternoon a special children's service was hold, presided over by the Rev T Bishop. The lesson was read by the Rev W C J Neville, and an address upon the word " Hero " was given by Mr Cathay, who was list mei to with marked attention by the crowded assembly. Miss Carrie Hastings delighted the congregation with her rendition of " The Holy City," whilst Mr R H Pearson played the violin solo " Ave Maria" (Gsunod), with his usual taste and skill. T,ne chapel was crowded at the evening service, the sermon by the Rev R Culley heing based upon the words" That which is to come,'"Phe anthem "Come unto Me" (Dr Warwick Jorlanl, was well rendered by the choir' with the following parts :—Soloa, Miss EandTaylor and Mr G Gough ; quartet, the Misses Plimpton and Kelly, Messrs {Varhurton and Hatch. Mr Levi Richardson gave an especially fine rendering of " In Native Worth "(Haydn). Praise is due to Mr Frank Hickman, who undertook to prepare the scholars for the anniversary, and who also presided at the organ. The collections amounted to £45.

DEATH OF MR EDWARD AARON.
OF WESTON.

At Mersey View, Weston. on Saturday morning Mr Edward Aaron passed away at the age of 73 years. The deceased gentlemtn for s)me tune ntd suffered from weakness and had been coofined to his bed for some weeks. About a month ago deceased was getting out of bed when he fell on his side and fractured two of his ribs, which led to his death. 17/ceased Coo 2— mericedgfrork as a bcy at Johnson's soapery and eventually became manager of Weston works. Be retired in September 1880. For over thirty years the deceased gentleman had berved the public well in many capacities. He bad been a member of the Board of Guardians, the old Highway Board, and the Rural District Council. A Ktrong churchman be was identified with the Weston Church and at one time with the Holy Trinity Chinch.,

THE INQUEST. - . On Monday morning, at the Royal Oak liotel,Weston, Mr:lt Dobson, district c 'toner, held an inquest touching the circumstances attending the death of Mr Aaron. Edward Aaron, son of the deceased, and living at Aigburth. Liverpool, stated the: his father was formerly rnanavr at the Weston Cneinical Works. He retired some years ago. He bad tr.2en attended by Dr Cum:berg, and died on Saturdav at 555 a.m. Oa the 3rd April deceased, who had a difficulty in seeing, re- tired to bed, and he was getting up again when he fell on his side on a chair by the bedside. It was subse- quently found that he had fractured two ribs. Dr Carruthers, of Ffaltoo, said he had b?en attending the dec..ased regularly for about a year and a half for paralysis, which chLfli, affected his legs, so that he could only walk with assistance. Orr April 4th witness was sent for in the morning, and was told that deceased had fallen against h niece at furniture in getting out of bed. fie examined him,and Lund that he had two ribs broken on the right side. Ile was very ill, suffering from the shock of th;) fall. The ribs united, but the paralysis gradually increased, and he became weaker. Death took place on Saturday morning. Ile considered that death was due to paralysis, hastened no doubt by the fall and the injury he received in April. The jury returoed a verdict in accordance with the medical evA Ince, and the Coron,r, as ee.ired by them, expressed sympathy with Airs Aaron and the family ira their sad bereavement.

div.head: Mr. E. J. Guest and the Education Bill. "Trfing to Capture the Children."
div.p: Mr. E. J. Guest and the Education Bill. "Trfing to Capture the Children."

A meeting of Sunday School teachers and eldw scholars was held in the schoolroom on Monday evening and, consideriug the circumstances, the attendance was satiafactery. Mr E J Guest, BA, presided, and was supported on the platform by the Revs 11 Cullsw , T Bishop, and W Neville. After devotional exercises, The CLIAIR3fAN in commenting upen the attendance, said that conaidaeing the beautiful night. and the unrest which the declaration of peace—thank God—had caused it was rather to be wondered at, perhaps, that they (his hearers) were there at all. T(l9 training of the young was one of the most important subjects that they could discuss—he did not know of any more important matter that could be brought before the mind of man. Parente had a tremendous reaper slaility in the training of their children, and he consinered that it was their duty to develop the physical, mental, and apiritual interests of the children in every possible way I Unfortunately there were many parents who were on I fit,ed fOr Uric wGrk, and the 7 delegated their ditties to ' othell. Sunday school teacherS vt&tl takkg ita the reapensibilities of parents to a large extent, and were doina work for which they (the parents) were un- qualified, or which th,y wem unwilling to do. He thought there were some weaknesses in connection with their Sunday schools, and one was that so many ycesece men an I young women who were qualified by education to undertake the work, were absent from the Sunday schools. He was also of the opinion that FOTIS Of those who were eneaged in tee work did not re alias thsir responsibilities and the necessity for hard work in order to make the Sunday schools successful. He thought Sunday school work would become more And more haver:ant in this country, eopecially if the Educe tionßill which was now in committee, were passed. The Nonconformists of this country would have Co wake up and make as much use as possible of the Sunday Scheola to counteract as much as possible the probable evil effects of what he thought was an iniquitous Bill, which the Free Churchmen should oppose to the very utmost of their power. There was not a doubt that the Anglicans and Romanists were trying to capture the children. They were net content to teach the childran their dog. mas on the Sunday, but they wanted to have them the whle week through. He thought it was most unfair that the taxes and rates of the country should go to a dominant church, for the instruction of ' the children in thess things in which they (the Noncon- formists) did not believe, Teey would be called upon to par for the teaching of that which they utterly re- pudiated. It was a very wrong Bill Indeed and would give a power to the Anglicans and Romanists in this country that the Free Churchmen would leave to fight against for years to come. (Applause). An address was then delivered by the Rev R Culley, whore subjsct was ~ What is essential and desirable in modern Suuday schools ?" He referred to the declara- tion of peace, and said they euasit all to be affected by it. 'Lae man who was not affected that night,whatever might be his political views, was past reasoning with. One thing surprised him, and that was that when an Englishman got excited he first of all ran to the public- house. That was a very extraordinary thing and he wished they co aid do something to prevent it. ! He thanked God that peace bad been proclaimed, and prayed that a settled Government might be given to South Africa. Continuing he said he took a very san- guine view of the future of the work of the Sunday schools. Ele was very glad to say that during the past year they had had an incrra ,e of over 6,000 scholars. (Applause.) The object of a Sunday school were three- f -Id—to lead the eaaildren to Christ, to train them up within the Church and not outside, and to teach them right conduct or the ethics ef Christian'tr. The first qualification of a Sunday achool teacher was supreme love. of the Lord Jesus Christ: The second qualification was the love of children, because three quarter 3 of the scholar 3 were children. Continuing the speaker said he considered that the art of training a human soul was a finer art than painting, I music, poetry, or sculptury. It was the finest of fine 1 arts. Referring to the Education Bill the rev gentleman I said he hoped Is strenuous eff ert would be made to " doctor it up," but when they had. done their utmost he was afraid, from the Nonconformist standpoint, the Bill would be almost hopelessly had. He wanted Hug- laud to grapple with the great ,21ubject of eincation instead of wrangling about tele ism and that ism, and do all they could to make up their minds to have the best system of elementary education to fouud in the world. Mr Caney impressed open his hearers the necessity of teaching as interestingly as possible, and handling the boys with tact. The problem of the Sunday Schools was the hobble-de-hoy—the lad in middle teens. Many boys bad slipped out of. th&r hands, whereas if they had been properly handled, they could have been retained. Mr W Sucoca proposed a vote of thanks to the Chair- man and speaker. Mr Culley, he said, held the position of Secretary to the Sunday School Union, and the words that fell from his lips were a coerce of inspiration to them all. Their friend Mr Guest was deeply interested in the question of education, and it had been a pleasure to have him presiding Over that meeting'. Mt PERKINS seconded, and the motion was heartily carried,

div.head: PEACE REJOICINGS.
div.p: PEACE REJOICINGS.
EARLE3TOWN AND NEWTON.

Ths welcome tidings of peace reached Earleatown at fire minutes to seven o'clock on Sunday night, when a telephonic message was received by Messrs Vickers. The flag was immediately hoisted and the works bell was curia. Stokera were surnamed and the furnaces were fired up in order that the st aim buzzer could be , put in eporation. The news spread rapidly, and instantly the wnole town bore; into calour, flags and hunting making their app?arance almost from every house. People turned out into the streets and when the sever sl churcoes and clatpels released their congregations the thoroughfares became impassable The chorus of steam whistles, the changing cf bells, and the various other noises expressive of joy all contri- buted to make a perfect pandemonium. The Viaduct Baud was requisitioned and they marched to the Market-square, where a crowd of four or five thousand people assembled. The bandsmen had considerable difficulty in pushing their way through the surging mass. Mr at Molyneux conducted , the proceedings and th7es or four hymns were sung in thanksgiving. Nothing could have been more impressive , and sublime, the whole of the assembly singing with great heartiness. For same time afterwards the tawn remained in an excited but happy state. At Newton the new b,lls of St. Peter'a rang out merry peals. Earlestown certainly never looked prettier in its history Clan it did on Manday. There never was such a galaxy of colour ; the whale town was ablaze with flags and bunting. The weather, too,seemed to have joined in the universal rejoicing and summer as well as peace had come at last. It soon became evident teat no one had the rem otest intention of working that day. The whole township turned out in its haliday attire. All the works closed for the day and the shopkeepers.tafter vainly endearorring to do buainess.were compelled to abandon it and jin in with the rest of the holiday makera. The Earlestown band were early astir and played selections of music in various parts of the to we. At 10.30 a thanksgiving servic was held in St John's Church, where there was an overfliwing congregation. , Afterwards a procession, consisting of many of the I characters who Cock part in the May festival on Satur- day, was arranged. The procession which was ex:en- ded ever a distance of 150 yards, went by way of :War- grave-road, to the Vulcan village, then by Cemetery- road to Newtcn,through High-street, Crow-lane, back to Market-street. On the Market-square several hymns were sung to the accompaniment of tne band, who, at the request of the people, played time after time the , National Anthem. In the afternoon the children who took part in the procession were regaled with light re- freshments at the Legh•street Mission Hall, the Rev J C Matthews, Messrs Brown, Openshaw, and Haynes, kindly assisting to entertain tam. Amusements were afterwards provided, and the youngsters spent a very enjoyable time. In the afternoon Mr Louis Forster sue- ceasfully sent up a number of fire-balloons, and in the eve fling the Market-square was the scene of a pyro- technic display, rockets and other fireworks acing die- charged. -ea RECET r OF TBE NEWS AT RUNCORN.

The announcement that peace had been signed arrived at Runcorn atout 8 o'clock, the news first being circu— lated by the blowing of Bolton's buzzer, Widnes, which, in turn, was taken up by syrens,whiatles,and "buzz rs " on the Runcern side. The bells of the Parish Ciunrch were quickly set ringing,andln an incredibly short time aCel. the good new tad been bruited about, the etre:de; were fill ,c 1 with re vie. St Edward's Catholic band also paraded the streets , those of a demonstrative disposition falling in the rear. 'On Monday the in ,jnity of the shops and the side streets were bedecked with bunting. At the National Church Schools the scholars were massed outside and sang several patriotic songs. le the evening there was a repetition of the SCP,IT'S witnessed on Sunday night the crowds massing in D ,vonshirs Square and the Market Place where several patriotic demonstrations took place.

div.head: REFERENCE AT Tin pErrY SESSIONS.
div.p: REFERENCE AT Tin pErrY SESSIONS.

I At the Runcorn Pty Sessions, on Monday morning IMr F J Norman, the presiding magistrate made the following speech :—Befors proceeding with the ordinary business ot the Court, let tale ash you to join with me in thanking God that peace has been restored. It would be ungenerous at such a time to refer to the Cause or conduct of the war. Thank God, it is over. May He comfort the poor snirowing ones who hove lost their loved ones in the conflict, and by on us the solemn obligation to care for the poor fellows who have been maimed in the fight. Rather let us now strive to show to our brave foes that they have been fighting against their best friends ; to prove to them that now they have , become fellow-subi-mts of our mighty Empire, they will I enjoy a nobler freedom and a larger hope than they ever I knew before. L=t us give them hearty welcomes and extend to them without grudging those glorious and political civil rights and religious liberties "broad based on which our mighty Empire stands," feeling confident that when they Come to realizo these przeless blessings they will vie with us in loyattv to the greatest King, iand patriotism to the grandest Empire the world has ever seen. God save the King.

div.head: RUNCORN BOARD OF GUARDIANS.
div.p: RUNCORN BOARD OF GUARDIANS.

At the close of the mneting. of the Runcorn Board of Guardians, the chairman, Mr A 11 Norman, T.P. said that that was;the first meeting held since they had br CaCcil id7vda ot tiset i27SdauntehwsAoffritch: f df threetb e years. strife whith As a public body they were delighted that this sad calamity he thought they co.:I I use those words—had come to an end, ho felt sure every one of them would feel a dense of deep gratitude towaris those brave fellows representing them at the front who I had been instrumental in b:inging the war to an end. At the same time he felt sure he wag only voicing the 1 feelings of all when he raid they respected the °rave Boers who bad stood up as they had for their cause from the own Standpoint in such a plucky way. It was a blessing that the war had COrEln! to an end and he hoped that Briton and Br would henceforth live together as brothers, which would be a happy termination of tne whole strife.

CLAIM AGAINST A CYCLE AGENT
Case at Warrington County Court.

- Attbn Warrington County Court,on Thursday, last before his Honour Judg,s Bowen Rowlands, Thomas Patrick Rigby, builder and joiner, Wilders- p3ol-road, brought an action ageinst David Guest, cycle agent, Mersey-street, to recover £6 ss, the price of a tandem bicycle, There was a counter- claim amounting to ..£1 53 for work done and materials supplied to a tandem bicycle,to the order of plaintiff.—Mr E A Connor appeared for the plaintiff, and the defendaut was represented by Mr TS Steel. Mr Connor said that at the boginning of September, 1901, Mr Guest called at plaintiff's business premises to see about some work he required doing, and there saw the tandem bicycle in question. In the early part of October defendant arranged to buy the tandem from the plaictiff for £6 5,, and took it to his shod en Mersey-street. Later in October the plaintiff sent defendant au invoice for £.6 Si, sop the money not having been paid, he forwarded another bill on December 4th. N 3 notice was taken of this.and plaintiff galled on the deferdant and asked him for pay- ment of the money. Defendant said he could net pay the money then, but would let him have it in the course of a fortnight or so. Dr fendant did not keep his promise and plaintiff again saw him in February. Defendant then mentioned that the back stass of the machine were weak, and plaintiff told him that as he had b ,ught the tandem be would have to settle that questioa for himself, Plaintiff again called during the following month, and defendant said he could not see his way to keep the tandem, and asked plaintiff to take it back again. Plaintiff agreed to take the machine back, pro- vided that it was put in the same order as it was when was taken by the defendant, Defendant agreed Co his, and plaintiff subsequently called for the tandem, when be was told by the defendant that be could rvlt have it until be had paid 15s for repairs which had been done. Plaintiff resented this, and proceedings were instituted. Mr Steel said his case was that the tandem was sent to Mr Guest, who: was reqtveted tot do certain repairs in order to make it saleable, and to tri, and find a' customer for it. Defendant did this and plaintK re- fused to pay for the repairs when defendant was unab'e to End a customer. Plaintiff having given evidence ia support of his cass, the hearing was adjourned.

div.head: NOTES ON UAMES AND ATHLETICS.
div.p: NOTES ON UAMES AND ATHLETICS.
Cricket.

Warrington experienced hard lines in not being able to record a victory as the result of their encounter with Cheethars. On Saturday as it was the match ended— luckily for Cheetham—in a draw' but it is gratifying to know that the Warringtonians have not yet had to submit to defeat this season. Saturday's engagement was decided at Manchester, and as both teams had been unbeaten previously this season, a keen contest was anticipated.

The Warrington captain won the toss, and Connor and Hawtin were deputed t open the innings, the bowling being shared by Parker and Allen. Cautious play was the order for some time, and the first hit of note was a fine drive by Connor off Parker. The score rose steadily, and at 20, T Sinclair took the ball from Parker, but the separation was effected by Allen, who made a successful appeal for Connor being lbw.

J Callon had only a brief stay,but Hawtin had a use- ful partner in .1 Gibbon. The new corner batted excellently, infusing plenty of power into his strokes whilst Hawtin hit out freely on several occasions. The aggregate reached 44 before Gibbon was bowled for a useful dozen. B Silcock came next and assisted to add 16 for the fourth wicket when Parker,who had relieved Sinclair at 50, got him caught at cover point.

Lynes now went to the wicket and showed a disposi- tion to hit, driving Naylor to the ropes. Hawtin con- tinued to bat steadily, but at 75 he returned one to Parker, who held the ball at the second attempt. Mr Hawtin's contribution of 25 was a faultless one marked with unusual patience and judgment. Six runs later the Warrington captain was taken at short slip, A mis- understanding cost Briggs his wicket at 90, whilst two runs later Lynes was bowled by a yorker after contri- buting a bard hit 18. W 11 Podmore added seven for the la.t wicket when he was bowled by Alleu, the innings closing for 99.

The Cheetham Eleven commenced their task with W R Sinclair and G Porter, the bowling being shared by Lynes and JIV Bibby. The amateur maintained a capital length and runs were hard to obtain. An over- throw augmented the score by five runs and the aggre - gate had reached 22 when Porter got his leg in front of a straight one. T H Sinclair joined his brother and at 29 saw his brother jump out to drive Bibby, miss and fall a victim to Hampson's dexterity behind the stumps.
Matters went badly for the locals now, and after Lynes had bowled Parker off his pads at 34, two wickets fell Hawtin taking Sharp at mid-off

whilst Bibby bowled Sowden all over his wicket. A run later Phasey was taken by Hawtin Naylor assist- ed Sinclair to stop the rot which had set in and added a dozen for the seventh wicket when he made a half hit and was beautifully taken by Podmore at cover. A run later a successful appeal by Bibby sent Sinclair back, and the match was looked upon in the light of a certainty for the visitors.

E. Collinge and W. Allen, however, batted steadily, and the excitement grew intense as the score steadily, mounted and there was a prospect of the batsmen saving the match. Connor took the ball from Lynes at 67, whilst in the last few minutes W. Podmore was tried. The total was taken to 80 when Allen was caught:at the wicket. Robinson whipped in and success- fully negotiated the last two balls,Cheetham thus luckily making a draw. Bibby bowled splendidly his capture of six wickets for 28 runs being a very creditable performance.

div.head: LATE fiR. THOMAS
div.p: THE LATE fiR. THOMAS
HAWTHORN.
Memorial Servide.

At Wycliffe Congregational Church, Warrington, on Sunday evening, a memorial service for the late Mr Thomas Hawthorn, a deacon of the church, was held. There was a large congregation. The Rev J Yonge preached an inepreseive retomeriil sermon based on the text : " A pillar in the ttmple of my God," 113yelations 3c., part of verse 12. This was a promise, be said, of the great future. What the greatness of its reality would our imaginations were hardly capable ef con- jecturing. The worldling went to nothing across tits river tut shame and contusion of face. But the servant of Christ went to everlasting honour and reward and blessedness. The pillar of the church on earth was sure to be made a pillar in the temple of our God. Hs took that text because when he came to think of some scripture appropriate to the servant of Jesus Christ who had just gone from this church on earth to his reward, no teat so aptly fitted his case. All who knew him best agreed with those who knee, him least that Thomas Hawthorn was " a pillar "in that church. From the very first of his connection with it he was strong in his attachment to it. He manifested that attachment and rendered his support in every way that was poileible ti him. The interests of Wycliffe were very dear te his heart. Ha was never so happy as when he Was jfisieg in the worship, listening to the truth, working in the school among the little ones, sharing in the ceuncile of both church and school, giving his time and hie thought, and his presence and bis sympathy te whatever concerned that place and peop'e. He found his greatest recreation there. He did not mind what or how much he did, or how many times on Sunday, or during the week, he had to come there. From the first of the P.S.A. he enlisted into its service and continued until physical strength failed him. NI deacon of the church had been more unremittingly constant. Hardly ever did he miss a deacons' meeting. Hardly ever did he miss a week- night service or a church meeting, or a com- mittee of which he was a member. He was not only thus constant in hab't, but he also displayed , confiderable Bout:dem of judgrar nt in all the affairs of the church. Be was a wise councillor. He gave the best of •himself to Wycliffe Church with unstinting diligence. Reliable to the full, steedfat.t, sympatisetio, loyal, a strength to his minister and his brethren, and he Cdr Yonge) did not hesitate ts) say, an example to the men, epecially to the younger men of that church. He deserved to be called a pillar of that church. And he was so consistent ; true to the profession that he made. Neither in speech tier in cenduct did he ever cast discredit upon himself as a men, or upon the church of which he wee known to be a member. !S.:item/8r he was so modest and unassuming. He never created hostile criticism net called attention to himself in any way. Easy to get on with,pleasant to confer will, a fellow worker that they not only had held in honour but in affeetion. The faithful servant, who had been so true a" pillar" of this church, the Lord had now made a pillar In the Temple of God, and be shall ge no more out. "Being dead, he yet speaketh " to his family, his fellow-members, his brother discuss, his pastor, to the young men of Wyciffe, to the scholars In the school, to the men of the P.S.A. If they would become " pillars "hereafter is the Temple in they must find their apprenticeship:hero. G needed many to follow in that worthy euecession. They wile were in the service must be stimulated to larger fidelity, and they who were not as yet enlisted in the faith and kingdom of Jesus, to them this departure appealed. Lee them make that tour the time of their submission and isonseeratien. The brother who was gone would urge ' that appeal. And the Master, who loved and needed them, called them to His service. The choir then sang the anthem "N. shadows yoadv."

The MAYOR said that, as the Council were aware, be bad the honour, as representing the County Borough of Warrington, of an invitation to the Coronation celebra- tions, and last week whilst in London he went to allCU- tain at the Earl Marshal's office whether it would be possible for him to attend the celebration at the Abbey. He saw the secretary of the Earl Marsh sl, and though he vary kindly intimated that it would give the Earl Marshal and the authorities great pleasure to see the representative of Warrinotoa at the Coroaation celebra- tion, he personally could out recommend his (the Mayor's) attendance owing to the difficulty of getting !to the seats in the Abbey, which were both up and downstairs, to anyone wh., was not able to I get abnut. Councillor Jamas EVANS, at the request of the War- rligtou Trades and Labour Connell, moved :—" That it be aa iastruction to all committees of this Council, is the event of any dispute with the employes of the Ger- proration, that the official representatives of the men shall °endue all interview' and arrange terms on their behalf." la soraking to the motion be said be did not propose to trouble the Council with many observations. This principle involved in his motion was one that had been adopted by several towns quite ea large as War- rington, and parhaps, as important. He could not give a complete list, but he knew. that Salford, Manchester, Belton, and Bury had accepted the principle, and to accent it was no nAw thing for Corporations in Laccathire as well as other countiM. was a matter of claiming a right. The law of the country recognized the right of combination, and he supposed that the members of the Wlrrington Trade and Lobaur Council claimed 'the right of representa- tion. He might say one word in explanation of the resolutioa. Flo did not wish that any portion of it should be misunderstood. The explanation of it was simply that the aesociation desired that employs. sheuld lathe event of dispute have the right of representation. Sup- posing a difference arose between the employes of the Council and the committals who had to do with them, they sought to have the right, without endangering the poetic:on of nay roan employed, to send a delegate or relegate the matter to a representative who would have power to off-ct the settlernint of that difference. The DEPVTT MAYOR dill not wish to vote on the reso- lution in the form in whish it was submitted by Counnillor Beam It was a matter that appealed to him very strongly, and he would respectfully suggest that Instead of opposing this resolution they should refer the matter to the General Purposes Committee for considera- tion and report. Dee way in which the resolution was shafted would snake the settlement of ally dispute com- pulsory in the way indicated in the resolution. There would be ne ether way of settling a dispu'e except through the official representative of the men—not the men themselves—,n the 0110 hand and the committee on the other. He did net think that was the intention if the Warrington Trades and Labour Council, and was not the intention of Councillor Evans, who had moved the resolution. As an alternative, though he would not be in order in moving it, he suggested a resolution which he thoueht would meet the require- ments of those interested. He then read the following : rest, in the event of any difference or dispute arising between any section of the employes of the Corporation cad any committee of the Council and ire the eveat of such difference or dispute not having been settl2d by personals intercourse betwett: the employes and the committee eionterned, the employee shall have the option if being represented in subsequent interviews by such person or persons as they nsty appoint." He submitted that that was a batter resolution than the one moved. Re thought the relations which existed with the men should be as personal and as friendly as possible. Ile suggested, th ' erefore that the matter should be referred to the General Purposes Committee lin order that some similar alternative resolution to that I which he had suggested might be recommended.

_ Allerrnan SUTTON said that with all due respect Councillcor Evans should become a moat popular man by taking up these questions. (Ltughter). Councillor Evan : I take a decided objection to such invidious obaervationt.

AltirMlU SUTTON, continuing, said he did not sea the necessity of such a resolution. If there shonld be a dis- pute or misunderstanding between the Corporation and their employes he did not think that on any question the Council would refuse to listen ta tho arguments of tho representatives of the men. Ho thought, there- fore, that they should not be bound down to the terms of the resolution in oil cameo, and

s Alderman Roberts had very properly put it, it bound them down to the determination of the official represent- atives of the men to conduct all interviews and fix all terms, which he did not think would be a fair thing to the Corporation. He thought that hitherto they had dealt with toe man in a vary satisfactory rnanner,and in any question be did not thiuk they would decline to hear the arguments of the representatives of the employee. Alderman SHAW Gauge said he thought the seltitien suggested by Alderman Roberts was a very helpful one, and suggested Councillor E9'4011 should withdraw his motion to permit of the course suggested tieing adopted. Councillor TINNIIN said he did not think there could be two opinions about ',easing a reseletioa in the spirit suregested by Alderman Roberts. and if a sort of under- taking could be given that it w said be discussed en those lines by the General Purpexes Committee, then it would be perhaps peseible for Councillor Evans to with- draw be resolution. The Council would admit that the' members of the various workmen's organisations had a perfect right to be represented by those whets, they would appoint, and that, to his mind, was all that was asked for in the motiors moved by Councillor Evans His own experience was that had the discussion ef diffi• culties in 11002.4 disputes been through the local secretary , or represeetetives of the men from the first, a greet deal of unpleseantness would be avoiCed. It was all vary well he Fay that the workmen should have the courage to urge their own claims, but it very often happened that" someone must be made a scapegoat," and this would prevent anything of that sort. Councillor F B ROBERTS said in his opinion the prin- ciple of the resolution proposed was to orec'es la the men from discessing suck questions in the first instance, and In this there was a very important difference of principle to that ongeneted by Alderman Rsberte. Alderman !totems also said he faveared the form sug- gested by Alderman Rebertt. Counalor Ivens Evatee, in his reply, expleined that 'he wee rather in a -difficulty as he was not respoisible for the teselution. but enle the mouthpiece of the Trade and Labour Council. He also intimated that he was not seeking p vularity in the way suggested by Alder- man Sutton. Alderman SUTTON I made no disparaging remarks. Councillor EVANS : No, but you made use of more ohjectioneble things still. (Laughter). Alderman SUTTON I said it WaS very kind of you to take up this case. (Laughter.) Ceueeiller Itvaws : YO9, exceedingly so ; and it is very kind of you to make the observations yen do. (Laughter.) On further remarks he intimated that he would withdraw the motion, provided the matter was disenssed by the General Purposes Committee as sug- gested, if he had then the option of moving a further resolution if necessary. The (pestle's was accordingly referred to the General Purposes Committee for consideration and report. A Plea for National Education Without Sectarianism. [TO THE EDITOR OF THB EXLMINER."] Sir,—Readers of newspapers cannot fail to be I impressed with the enormous correspondence that is now eoing on in reference to the Government Edueation Bill. But in this ens., as well al in many others, confusion and not wisdom is to be found in the multitude of coun- sellors. One thing, however. 'Perna to emerge from the fog of the controversy. Front the exultation of the friends of the Bill and the fears of its enemies, I think it may be inferred that the inteation of its framers is to play into:the hands of their clerical henchmen by extend- ing their control over the religious traieing of thelyoung. Nor woeld this infeetion be either unreasonable or unjust were the State Church a National and not a sectional iostitution. But when we remember that fully one-half of the people will have nothing to do with Episcopacy, then indeed the Church stands out prominently se a national injustice. And evefy attempt on the part of the Government to thrust its tenets upon unwilling minds should be treated as an impudent and unwarran- ted interference with the religious liberty of a free people. But what right, I ask, has Parliament, Tory or other- wise,to deal with a religious question at all ? Its members are chosen and elected as political and not as sew:arian partisans, and this is so thoroughly understood that the very name of God has no place in toe deliberations of the House. Bills affecting both the moral and material conditions ef men both at home and abroad are deb-uted and passed without any reference to Him whose Gospel Is said to be our natieual faith. Let me cite a case of this apparent abnegation of our Lord and Master. The war in South Africa, now happily ended, had both ita backers and opponenta in the House of Commons, but who has ever heard or read of Honourable Members standing up in their planes and defending or con lemm- ing the war upon the principles formulated by Christ. An assembly of 'nee governed by political partisanships, and legislating upon there lines alone, are not the people to be trusted to develop a scheme of rdigious education. And their incompetence for the task is rather emphasised than otherwise by the fact that there is great diversity In their creeds. A Bill for religious education deviied and exemated by ardent disciples of Anglic tnism, Romanians, Methodism, and other isms, and spiced with a little Nothingeriaoism would be a veer remarlrable document—a veritable Joseph's coat of many pieces and many bum But if Parliament, as at present constituted, has neither the right nor the fitness to legislate for the re- ligions training of our children it does not follow that it hie no duty to perform in the secular educatim of the country. It is a sore disgrace to a civilized state that any of its members should be ignorant of the rudiment- ary elements of human knowledge and therefore un- qualified for the proper disoharge of the duties of life. And as the happiness and prosperity of a nation very largely depend, under God, upon the intelligence and well ordered habits of its people, it is clearly the bounders duty of Rulers to do all in their power to pro- mote and encourage such intelligence and order. For this noble purpose sehools free from all denoneinationa- lime and supported entirely by the state, should be es- tablished in all our eitise, towne, villages, and hamlets where, under wall-trained and well paid teachers, the children and youths of the country might be thoroughly Instructed in the learning and arts requisite to prepare them for their respective occupations in the world. nth a system of education would sweep away the religious difficulty that has so long been a root of bitterness and a scandal to Christian people ; and its effects would Soon ha apparent in a higher tone and greater skill in all our workers. And who would demur to be taxed for this universal education; ! The nation now patiently bears the enormous burdens that are imposed upon it for the malevolent purpose of making war upon the weaker countriee. And surely it would willingly contribute the millions that might be required for the peaceful and more legitimate object of providing a national education that would improve the social con- ditions of the people, and enlarge their capabilicies for friendly competition with other nations in the indus- trial and commercial pursuits of life. If it be objected that the education I have shadowed forth is Godless,my answer is that there is nothing Godless in the world but the evil thoughts and evil deeds of men. All the phenomena of heaven and earth are full of the Almighty and it is said lathe Oracles that in Him men live and move and have their being. Surely then it would be a dishonouring of God to suppose that He would leave us through a system of education that would develop all our mental faculties and thus enable us to make the best use of the material blessings with which He has surrounded us.
------ I trust that no reader wall do me the injustice to infer from the foregoing that I 11113 opposed in any way to the religious instruction of the young, for assuredly I am

not. But what Ido most emphatically object to is the interference of the State to propagate sectarianism iP our 4011001 s. And my reason for this opposition is based kpan two ClOSlderati one, namely, the injustice of such interference, aid the knowledge that sectarianism and Christianity are two very diffe,eat things. The former divides Christian men it,t different camps, having little in common ; whcreaa the latter unites the followers of Josue into one concrete " little flock" who acknowledge no master and no teacher but Him. And after all, the relirioue training of our children is neither thelwork of Parliament or of priests. Religiona education, like charity, should begin at home. It is the imperative duty of parents t) train up their children in the way they shou:d go, and the sending of them to day and Sunday schools is but a sorry attempt to relieve thens- selves of that great and precious responsibility. The child loves and trusts its parents,and kind words and living commit at the fireside will du more to mould itS character for good than any other human agency.--e' Yours truly, June, 1902.

A Disputed Lease at Warrington.

At the•Warrington County Court on Thursday, last be- fore his Honour Judge Bowen Rowlands,K.C., Benjamin -Kenyon," Green Man" Inn, Green-street, brougut au I action against Samuel Davenport general dealer, to obtain possession of the two shops and dwelling-houses 30 and 32, Green-street, of which plaintiff is the owner, and which it was alleged, were held by the defendant as tenant up to the 16th December, 1901, at the weekly rental of 5s 4d and 4s 6d respectively, at which date notice to quit was given and the tenancy expired. Plaintiff also claimed the sum of £l3 7s 2d for rent and means profit'. Mr A Browne represented the plaintiff and Mr Rigby Swift, barrister (instructed by Messrs Spencer Wellhead and Son) appeared for the defendant, Briefly stated the plaintiff's case was that William Fairclougb, the testator, died on the 27th of August, 1871, and by his will be created certain life tenancies (1) to his son Thomas Fairclough (2) to his son's wife, Marv. Thomas Fairclough died on the 21st of June 1886. The defendant became a tenant of part of the property in 1880 and of a second portion in 1885. Mr IDavenport was a weekly tenant up to the year 1886. In this year the defendant alleged that the wife of Thomas Fairclough granted him a lease for 21 years. This lease Mr Browne contended, was a bogus one and was drawn up by an "amateur lawyer." Mr Swift : Does my friend suggest that it is a forgery ? Mr Browne : It was drawn up by an amateur lawyer, and the trustees of this estate never heard of this lease.

His Honour : Your case, Mr Browne, is that if this document or lease was granted, it was granted by the wife of Thomas Fairclough when she had no power to grant it, and that the document is void. Mr Swift: Mr Browne should not make these broad allegations of fraud against us. His Honour : The dispute is whether the lease was granted by Mary Fairclougb. Mr W D Jeans, jun, of the firm of Me6srs W D Jeans and Son, produced the deeds relating to the trust of William Fairclough, also the documents relating to the sale of the property to Mr Benjamin Kenyon on the 12th November, 1901. His firm had acted throughout in the trust and they bad no knowledge of the lease alleged to have been granted by Mary Fairclough to the defendant The price paid by Mr Kenyon was £1,200 for six shops. Mr Rigby Swift addressed the Court on bebalt of the defendant. In April of 18E0, he said, Mr Heaton of Warrington, one of the trustees, and also one of the pestle' who conveyed the property to Mr Kenyon in 1901, agreed with Mr Davenport to let him one of the shops in Green-street at 58 43 per week for a term of 10 years. Teat lease was signed by both trus- tees and Mr Davenport. It was drawn up by a clerk in the employ of Mr Heaton, named Joseph Mercer, the same individual who subsequently drew up the lease in dispute. In 1885, the same trustee let the other shop to the defendant Davenport fer 4s 9tl weekly, thus making a total rental of lOs ld for the two shops. In June 1886 Thomas Fairclough died, and about that time Mr Heaton , one at the trustees, approached Mr Davenport, and asked him if he would take a lease for twenty-one years of the two shops. He told Mr Daven- port that if he would do this he (Mr Heaton) would knock threepence per week off the rent. Defendant agreed to take the shops on the lease and the rent was reduced to 9s 101 per week. That agreement was carried out by a lease dated June 7th, bat the lease was not executed till much later than that date. From June 28th the alteration was made in the amount of the rent. fle contended that all along Mr Heaton knew that the lease was in existence, and he would call in- dependent witnesses who in 1897 showed Mr- Heaton the lease.

Samuel Davenport, the defendant,was then called,and stated that in the year 1880 he became the tenant of one of the shops on a lease from Mr Heaton. About five years afterwards he took the second shop. In June 1886 Mr Heaton asked him to tate the shops on a twenty one years' lease. Witness agreed to this and the lease was signed. He could not remember the date on which the lease was executed, but it was about the end of June A lady dressed in black, who he did not then know,but whom he subeequeetly learned was Mrs Mary Fairclough, was present wnen the lease was executed, and the lease bore the " mark " of Mrs Fairclough. The rent book showed that the reduction was made on June 28th. In 1897 Mr Heaton sag the lease. In cross-examiaation witness denied that he had put every obstacle in the way of plaintiff seeing the lease. Robert Lowe, estate agent, said that in July 1897 the defendant called upon him, in censequenee of having received a letter from Mr Cowciell, agent to Mr Heaton, with reference to the property, He brJught th e lease produced,which was in:the handwriting ofJosephM ercer a clerk who was then employed by Mr Heaton, to witness's office,and the lease was discussed at a meeting subsequently held at the office. Mr Heaton then saw the lease, and it was not suggested that it was invalid.: In answer to Mr Browne witness denied that the lease was snatched from Mr Heaton or Mr Co wdell by defendant or himself, before they had time to read it.
: . Ilas Honour asked if the case was incapable of solution otherwise Una by his judgment. It might be a very serious:matter. After further legal argument, Mr Browne called _ .

Mary Jane Emmett, daughtir of the late Mary Fair. dough, whc stated that at the time when the deed was alleged to have been executed her mother was an invalid. Witness, however, admitted that Mrs Fairclough was able to go out. Alderman Robert Hestcm then gave evidence. He denied that he ever approached Mr Daven- port to ask him to take a twenty-one years' lease Defendant approached him and witness told him that he could not have a lease as the trustees bad no power to grant one. Witness never instructed his clerk to prepare the lease. Mrs Fairclough never put her" mark " to any lease or document at witness's office. She had never been in the office in her lifs. Mr Davenport never &grad a document in the office in his (witness's) pre,enee. In 1897 he saw the defendact and told him that the rates of the property would be incre:.sed, and defendant then said he had got a lease. A time was appointed for witness to see the lease at Mr Lowe's office. He went to the office and a document was pro- duced, which he began to read, but the defendant saatched the paper away from him before he could read it. Witness did not know until last week that the lease had been attested by his clerk. He had never received a counter-part of the lease. In cross-examination witness said he did not tell the plaintiff before he bought the property about the inci- dent at Mr Lowe's office with regard to the lease. ale Honour, in giving judgment for the defendant, said he was of opinion that the deed of June, 1836, was Ithe deed of Mary Fairclough, and if it were necessary to pronounce definitely, he was satisfied upon the evidence adduced, that the deed was not executed on June 7th, but on a subsequent date. He would not discuss the , allegation made by Mr laeaton with regard to the meet- ing at Mr Lowe's office, except to say that he was not I satisfied that any such conduce was indulged in by Mr Lowe or Mr Davencort. Both these gentlemen were r entirely guiltless of any impropriety in their conduct during the interview. ThereEwould be judgment for the defendant with coats.

div.head: REV. E. 1. REED.
div.p: THE REV. E. 1. REED.

A Parting Gift from Emmanuel Church. A social meeting of the congregation of the Emmanuel Church, Warrington, was held in the schoolroom en Thursday last weak for the purpwe of presenting the Rev E. T. Reed with an illumin- ated address and a purse of money prior to the termination of his pastorate. The meeting was well attended and besides the members of the con- gregation there were present ministers of the various Free Churches in town,who joined heartily in tbeir expression of tribute to the worth and ser- vice of Mr, Reed. The Rev J L Milne sent a letter as he was unable to attend, also the Rev S Hughes who said" No minister of God could have had the welfare of his own church more at heart or laboured more ardently and conscientiously for the common weal or is held in higher esteem among the ministers of the Free Churches than your minister. We deeply regret his removal from the district, by his departure your church loses a good minister of Jesus Christ, the community at large a devout and zealous worker, and we a brother beloved." Mr Page(Vicar's warden) made the pre- sentation and Mr Atherton (people's warden) also spoke. Mr Reed very feelingly responded and said the severance had been on extremely trying one for him, but ke had taken that step in a spirit of love towards every member of the congregation with a sincere desire for their best interests. The address which was designed and beautifully finished by Miss Lees,reads as follows :—Emnaanuel Church, Warrington. Presented to the Rev Edward T Reed by the congregation of the above church on the occasion of his retiring from the pastorate which he has filled with a rare con- scientiousness and faithful devotion for over ten years,His ministry in Warrington will leave its mark for good. He has won the affection and high regard of his people by his kindly nature, his characteris- tic thoroughness and consistent walk and has ren.

div.head: MAN
div.p: MAN

At the Warrington Occasional Court on Tuesday, before Messrs John White and F A Frost, Thomas Jones, Houghton-street, Earleatown, was charged with attempting to commit a rape on Kate Eliza Webster, aged 17, of Ciarence-street, Newton, on May 26h.—After hearing the evidence, the magis- trates committed prisoner for trial at the Liverpool Sessioni, A SUNDAY NIGIIT SCENE AT GOLRGRNE—POLICE-
MN SAvAGELY ASSAuLTED.

At the Warrington County Sessions on Wednes- day, John and Patrick Waldron were charged with being drunk and disorderly in High-street, Gol- borne, on June 1 ; and also with assaulting Ser- geant Young and Police-constables Johnson and Wilde. Patrick Waldron was charged with a ' further assault on Sergeant Young at Golborne Police Station. Prisoners pleaded guilty. The Sergeant said that on Sunday evening the prisoners were creating a disturbance in High-street, Clai- borne. A large crowd had collected, and when be and the constables tried to persuade prisoners to go borne they refused, and John Waldron struck P.C. Johnson in the face. Patrick also was very vio- lent, and on being brought to the police-station be hit witness on the nose with something hard, caus- ing a severe wound. On the way to the police station witness received a stab in the thigh ; but be could not say whether the prisoners did it or not, He lost a large quantity of blood, and his trousers and tunic were both damaged. The prisoners were both very violent, and kicked and struck witness and the other constables.—Mvidence was given: by the constables and Superintendent Cocker asked the magistrates to deal severely with the prisoners and protect the police from such ruffianly assaults.—The Bench decided to send both prisoners to gaol for three months with hard laboar for the assault and to fine them 53 and costs or 14 days for being drunk

div.head: NOTES BY THE WAY AT EARLESTOWN.
div.p: NOTES BY THE WAY AT EARLESTOWN.

When the peace news reached Earlestown and Newton on Sunday evening, the streets, which at the time were soccewhat deserted, as if by magic became packed with excited crowds. Many won- dered if the rumour were true, but the ringing of the bells, the blowing of buzzers, and other mani- festations placed the matter beyond doubt, and al- though it was Sunday. the crowd gave themselves over to exuberant evidences of joy. Of course it was plainly evident that there would be no work next day, and this Wag proved to be too true when the works opened at six o'clock, for at the outset not more than about 20 men showed any inclination to start.

During the morning people began to muster on the Market square, and here a procession was soon formed including the majority of the characters who took part in the May Queen festival on Satur- day. The Viaduct brass band headed the procession which paraded all the chief parts of the township, much to the discomfort of many of the youngsters, who were very tired at the closs. Flags and bunt- ing were freely displayed and the town wore a bright and festive appearance.

Councillor Gilmour was highly plessel with his present the other evening, and he had every reason to be, as it was one ot which any man might be proud. It has been asked more than once whether this is to be a precedent. If it is I am afraid the contests for the position of District Councillor will be more keenly contested for than hitherto.

SILOCICENG CASE, OE CHILD NEGLECT AT WARRINGTON.--•-
PA9P:OrTs SP:NT TO GAOL.

Two cages of neglect of children have been investigated by Warrington magistrates this week. The first was heard on Wednesday, when Alice Coneannon, 238, Knutsford-road, wife of John Concannon. an en-ploye of the Corporation, appeared before Aldermen button, Monks, and Hutchinson on the charge of having neglected her three children In a manner likely to cause them unnecessary suffering and Injury to health —Mr Crompton appeared to prosecute on benalf of the N.S.P.C.C.. and stated that the husband was a very good man and raid his wife regularly 223 per week. The three children who had been neglected were Mary,seven years of age: Kate, six and John. four. They were well nourished but very dirty, being covered with vermin. Their heads were in a terrible condition. The state of the children was owing entirely to the prisoner's drunken habits. The society had given her every possible opportunity to reform, but she had given herself no to drink. The other day she actually pawned he hoots to anode her to get drink. It was the opinion of the society that no more chances should be given to her, but that she should be sent to prison.—lnspector Hackett deseriberl the condition of the house which was inn filthy state. When he last visited prisoner she was suffering from the effects of drink and was shaking badly.—Dr Pettcocke described the filthy condition of the children, and ha answer to the Clerk 'said it was brought about owing to neglect.—Prisoner was sent to gaol for a month.—The second case was heard on Wednesday, when George Henry Harrison. a puddler. living at 102. Pierpoint-strect. off Beweev-road, and his wite,Mary Ellen Harrison, were charged with neglecting their three children.—Mr IROOWne, who prosecuted on behalf of the ' said the man was a very hard worker, but his wife would not give up drink, and neglected the home and the children. The male prisoner bad made a statement to the'effeet that his children Were half-naked and their clothes filthy dirty" His wife bad pawned everything for drink. No rent had been paid since they had been in the house, and be feared every day that they would be turned out. On Saturday last he gave his wife 21s 6d ; but on Sunday there was no food in the house and he gave her Is extra to go out to buy food for the children.. He (Mr Browne) asked for the full penalty to be initiated on the womaz.—P 0 Leonard deposed to visiting the house in December and find- ing the children nearly naked, The woman was out,and tho house was in a filthy condition There was neither fire in the grate nor food in the house. The smell was horrible. mrs mstrisco subsequently returned, and she appeared to be suffering from the effects of drink.—P C Cooper said he visited the house on Ma Y 13th. The prisoner was in becliat 10.30 Si in. The bedroom was in a filthy state and stank horribly —P C Clough deposed to finding the prisoner drunk In the house. The mat tresses on which the family slept were not fit for a dog to lie upon.—James Marsh, with wh,)m the prisoners formerly lodged, said he blamed the man as ranch as the woman, because he was of dirty habits. and gave his wife no encouragement to be better.—lnspeetor Hackett gave evidence and said the man had from time to time com- plained about tris wife —Evidence for the male prisoner was given by his employer at the works, who expressed the opinion that Harrison WAS a sober man.—Mrs Harrison who has previously suffered imprisonment for the same offence. called a witness, who stated that the male prisoner was •' quite as bad "as the female, in fact, the worse of the two. —Prisoners expressed contrition, and said that if the Bench would "look over "the ease this time they would "turn over a new leaf in future." The Bench committed the vrisoners to gaol far three months.

div.head: MAY QUEFN FESTIVAL AT
div.p: MAY QUEFN FESTIVAL AT
-EARLESTOWN.

The festival inaugurated for the benefit of the building fund being raised for the extension of St John's Church, Earlestown, took place on Saturday afternoon in lovely weather. The proceedings took the form of the Coronation of the May Queen, and much time and labour were expended in making the affair a success. Most of those having charge of the demonstration were officials of Si John's Church, but the serretary, upon whom the bulk of the work fell, was Mr S Kilminster. The weather up to Saturday morning was not at all of an encouraging nature, rain falling until about 9 o'clock, but suddenly the clouds dispersed and the sun shone out brilliantly. Large crowds of people flocked into the town from the neighbouring tewns, and soon the streets be- came congested. The marshalling ground was the Market Square which had been kindly placed at the disposal of the Committee by the Urban Dis- trict Council and was enclosed with canvas. The streets wore a gay appearance, as on the cessation of the rain, a large number of premises were speedily decorated with flags and bunting, gay streamers being stretched across from side to side of the streets, Shortly before the advertised time of assembly, one o'clock, characters of various kinds began to arrive on the Market Square, and the mar- shalls, Dr Mouncey, Messrs G Dale, J Rylance, J Brown, and S Openshaw, were kept busily engaged in making order out of chaos. Prizes were offered for tradesmen's turnouts,and there was a numerous entry. The judges were Mr James Dodson of Huy- ton, and Mr Smith of Ormskirk. The adjudication was very carefully performed,and the awards were: —Local light turnouts: 1, Baskerville, Earlestown; 2, Sharpe, Earlestown; 3, Toft, Earlestown. Open; light turnouts: el, Norman Bros, St Helens 2, J Paythian, St Helens; 3, J Kerr, St Helens. Local heavy turnouts: 1, 3 Fairclough, 2, Sankey Sugar Company; 3, W Cawley. By the time the judging had been completed the pageant was ready to move. It was really a very brilliant affair. The promoters had promised to endeavour to surpass other festivals of a similar character, and they certainly name very near doing so, the procession quite exceeding all anticipations. As had been previouely announced the honour of the Queen of the May had been conferred upon Miss L Clayton who upheld her regal state with dignity. Her Coronation robes were .of beautifully figured silk, trimmed with beads, gold braid and white silk. flanging from her shoulders was a full court train of crimson plush, lined with silk trimmed with ermine and fastened with ostrich tips. Her slippers were of white satin. She carried a very charming bouquet of white roses and maiden hair fern. She, with her lady in waiting (M as L Dale,occupied a carriage drawn by four greys (sup- plied by Mr I Haskins). The dress of the lady in waiting was of white silk trimmed with lace, and puce velvet collar trimmed with ermine. Masters Bertie Ball and Percy Haynes were the pages in attendance, and Masters W Pope and F Houghton were the train bearers. They were arranged in all the glory of red plush and bright buttons. The maids of honour, the Misses Openshaw, Bowker, Green, Waterman, Faulkner, Naylor. Glinn and Adams, were drawn in a 'carriage and pair, also supplied by Mr Haskins. Their costumes were similar to that of the lady-in-waiting, the only difference being they wore very pretty wreaths of forget-me-note. The Queen's carriage was:preceded by the sword bearer (Master C the sceptre bearer (Master H Brown) and crown bearer (Master Hod- nett), who were respectively arrayed in blue, purple, and red plush. The crown was a very pretty piece of work, consisting of crimson plush, ornamented with imitation gems and pearls, and trimmed with ermine. Some very effective tableaux followed, the violet and primrose queens being especially admired. The following was the order of the procession : Mirshals (mounted)

The number of childran-who took part was 1,100. The procession left the Market-square by way of Haydock-street, and proceeded along Cross-lane, Crow-lane West, to the top of New road, Market- street, into Lord-street, Legh-street, Viaduct-street, Earle-street, Queen-street, King-street, Bridge- street, Market-street, Oxford-street, to the ground. ground the judges gave their decisions in the tableau and character classes, which were as fol- lows : Tableaux: 1, Violet Queen (Miss Seton) 2,Rock of Ages(Miss Annie Lythgoe); 3,White Slave (Miss Broster). After the march round the ring, the Queen, with her retinue, was escorted to the throne, which was covered with a pretty canopy, and as she ascended the steps the Earlestuwn Band contributed a selec- tion of music. Britannia then took her seat on the Queen's right hand. The chief function of the festival—the crowning of the Queen and the pre- ' sentation of the sceptre—was performed by Mrs Clare, of Latchford. and in doing so she said " Lily Clayton, I Crown you Queen of the May. I hope your Majesty will be happy and prosperous, and that your subjects Will remain loyal and faithful.' The performance of the ceremony was greeted with loud applause from the four or five thousand spectators, and the band struck up " God save the King." Mrs Clare subsequently. presented the Queen with a pearl necklace with diamond clasp, and a morocco- bound church service. There was the usual presentation of subjects, followed by the Maypole dance. The children danced the pretty and intricate step with great skill and the ribbons were effectively plaited. The per- formers had been trained by Mr J Brown, who bad also instructed another contingent in a charming skipping rope dance with which they entertained the company. Another feature of the Coronation festivities was the Highland dance by 32 artistes in national dress The children had been trained by Mr S Openshaw. An entertainment by a minia- ture troup of minstrels was a very attractive item of the proceedings, Dancing was subsequently in- dulge t in and the proceedings were maintained until dusk. The committee had received a great deal of valuable help, the several works and many trades- people lending horses, lurries, &c. The platform

Here was a proof, without any words that the Church of England was the head, and they couldn't put it behind. (Laughter.)
