The TowN Cutex : The Education Bill is now in Committee, and any recommendations ought to be made without delay. .

-Councillor 13ENNETT thought the representatives of the Church of England were entitled to the deciding voice in the management of schools which they bad erected. With respect to the religious difficulty be would be glad if some such arrangement as that which existed la Scot- land could be carried ou in this country. He did not see why certain bur a could not beallotted to representatives of particular denominations for religious teaching: Ho wanted to see absolutely fair play on every side. (Hoar, hear.)

Councillor F 11 ROBERTS said he could not understand how Aldtrnasn Roberts and Councillor Bennett could support the resolution, because thsir suggestions were abiolutely in opposition to the general principles of the SW. It was because of the unfortunate woreing of the resolution that he felt bound to record his cooseientious opposition to it. Tne geutlernen who hsd already spoken were not within a mile of plumbing the depths of the seriousness of this most serious question. For instance Councillor Bennett spoke with et certain amount of levity about people who supplied the buildings being entitled to manage the schools. Because they supplied the baildinge and thereby, he supposed, saved the rate- payers a certain amount in ponn is shillings and pence, they were to manage not the maintenance of the fabric or the erection of an annexe, bat they were to manage the entire religious education of the school. councillor Bennett's argument amounted simply to this—that they as Nonconformists were to sacrifice their most eerneet convictions—convictions for whin their ferefethere had struggled and suffered—simply because the Established Church in some 8,000 villages was going to supply the bricks and mortar within which the childrea would be housed. He could only say that if they were }going to purchase proselytisation and other very objectionable things, if they were going to r:sk odium theelogium in its very worst and most aggrayat form for the sake of a yearly reatal of buildinee, they were guilty of treachery te their principles which they had not been guilty of, as far as his memory and the reading of history went, fr centuries past. Be objected to the general principles of the Bill, first because he did not believe in taxation without adequate representation. Some might ask what difference did it make ? It would make all the difference between abeolute freedom of religious conviction, and the swallowing of the religious prindiples of people with whom they did not agree. It made no difference, in his view, whether the managers of schools who were nesninateS by the church had an absolute majority of two-thirds or a mere majority of one. His contention was that if the ratepayers were going to furnish the funds to maintain the schools, the ratepayers ought to have absolute government; and management of the schools so sup- ported. (Hear, hear.) That principle had been ad- mitted in English government for a very long time and it was the first time for many years that any qaostion had been raised as to putting it aside. The Govern- ment had no right to ask them to pay a single penny unless the ratepayers bad not merely seven-eighths, or nine-tenths of the management of the schools, but the entire management. If they used the Church schools in the villages they must pay a rent for them. The promoters of the Bilehowever, did not claim to man- age the schools because tney supplied the fabric, the in- tention was to manage the achools that they might supply the doctrine. (dear, hear and "No, no.") To that, he, as a Dissenter, objected and should object, and he most earnestly protested against the resolution before the Council. He supposed it was well known to the mem- bers of the Council that there were eB,OOO villages in Which the only school was a school belonging Co the Church of England. Children of those "alleges must attend the Church school. It was all very well to say, as Coancillor Bennett said, that the parents of these children ought to be strong-minded enough to demand separate religious/ instructioa for their children, but he thought he could show Councillor Bennett and that Council that the parents were put in a very difficult and even a very dangerous position, by making any such demands. (" No.") He said they were, and he w3uld prove it. They (Ms hearers) would say that the Bill made provision for these parents, for it distinctly said that if there were thirty children in any village whose parents demanded a school of their own, the ratepayers would be bound to provide education in that school. If the parents were in a position to provide the fabric, the ratepayers must supply the funds necessary for the teaching equipment of the school. They (his hearers) would say " Wnat can be fairer than that ?" He sedd it was not fair ; he said it was grossly unfair, for this reason. Who were the Dissenters in villages as a rule, and what was their social standing ? As everybody knew, who had worked in villages as he hed,Dissenters ie moot villages belonged to the very poorest classes. They were, as a rule, labourers on the estates of wealtoy landed pro- prietors or on the farms ef large farmers. Let them (his blarers) assume that ten parents as the fathers of thirty children put their heads together and demanded a school of their own what would heppen? Who would have to pay the increased rates, the doubling of the rates which would follow to enable the school to be built ? Very likely, the rich landowner, the large farmer, the employer, and the master over the very men who, as Dissenters demanded separate religieus instruction. Ho fancied that the ten unfortunate min would be summoned to the presence of the rich landed proprietor or the large farmer, and be told they could choose between sending their children to the Church school, or finding another job. Would any landed proprietor, or farmer in the world, coasent to these labourers—whose places could be filled to five minutei—Jemanding something which would double his (the employer's) rates. dm (the speaker) did not believe it, and he thought those labourers woull be given very short tariff iedeed, No amendment of the Bill, short of complete remsyta would satisfy him. This might be an irrecenciliable position. He knew it was. Fie i”lioved the Bill to he utterly and thoroughly bad. In a word, he believed, not because he was an atheist or an agnostic, but because he thought, be had some claim to being a Christian gentleman, but he believed from emviction that nothing short of secular education, pure and simple by the State, would end this religious difficulty. Tire seoner the clergy of the Chorales of England and Rome recognised this fact the better. The (the clergy) might now, probably would, win a brief triumph,but he was certainly convinced that they wore setting their beat dead against the stream of the tendency of the time. They were only laying up for themselves trouble, dislike, 'Rad contempt which they would reap hereafter. (Hear, hear.) Alderman SUTTON said it seemed to hina quite evident thst it would he perfectly impossible te come to any satisfactory decisien on the question. It was one of those questions which, he held, if they discussed for six mouths, they would be no nearer. He thought it Was a waste of time to diecuis it. (Hear, hear). Cadec tie circumstances he would just remark th st th 3 question had been discussed over and over again, and he under- stood it was referred to the Muse,urn Committee in order that they could submit to the Council what they cen- eider sd was the proper thing to do. That report had peen presented, and he thought the only thing they had to do wee to carry the resolution or leave it alone. Councillor TINNION was also of the opinion that it would be impossible to reconcile the diffsrepees which seemed to exist between the , members of the Council. There was no doubt that there were gentlemen who honestly believed that this was one of the best passible Billa, whilst others honestly telieved that it was not a good Bill, and no amount of discussion could alter those convictions. lie, as a Dissenter, could Inet support the Bill in its entirety, and not even in the half-hearted manner that the resolution proposed. The only good that would arise from the discussion was that it would shove the ratepayers that the educational matters of the future were of sueh vast impertance,aad that the powers that were likely to be given tie the Town Councils were so important that they (the ratepayers) would par considerably more attention to the selec- tion of the gentlemen who were likely to carry out the details of the Bill. Be was still in favour of School Boards; and he thought the best possible authority was an authority elected for that special purpose. He thought it would be wiser if the resolutions were with- drawn, as members would Simply vote Dissenters and Church, Liberal and Tory. Alderman SHAW GREEN Reid be would like lee avoid ! any further die:ousel:en. Alderman Bel:teens had offered such an excellent solution that they might.very properly adopt it. Be had told thorn of the very Wise and ! thoughtful observations that fell from the Archbishop of Cant,rbury, and he (the speaker) might add from the Bishop of Winchester, suggesting a conference. Hej (the Alderman) sugzested that the Ceuneil Instead of votint, on the present resolution, should ask the Museum i 'Committee to adopt the idea of eendiog forward the recnnernendation that the Council would like to see a 11 conferOect of all authorities interested in education, because what they desired to see, be took it, was A national system. We had already a most excellent system in the towns which had Board j Schools—none better in the world, he should think—but we nPeded something more than We already had, in Order to cope with the dangers that were ahead of us in the industrial competition with other nations. The very fact chat the principal members of the Liberal party,the Protestant Alliance (Archdeacon Taylor, of Liverpool being a very prominent and outspoken member, none having spoken, more thoughtfullylon the subject than he). the Trades Unions, the CO-operative movement in its annual gatherings and the whole of the Non-conformist I party of England were differing from the Bill,

Mr R Philpot, secretary to the Public IV3rks Loan Board, wrote, under date May 26 h, stating that the Board were prepared to investigate the application as regarded the sum required for works of sewage. The rate of interest at which the Board were at present empowered. pursuant to the Publics Works Loan Act 1897, to grant loans on security of local rates. repayable In not exceeding 30 years, was 31 per cent, per annum. If the Council desired to proceed with the application they should forward the sanction of the Local Govern- , meet Board b th 3 borrowing. THE THELWALL NIIISAN'CE AGAIN.

Mr R A. Naylor wrote from St. Michael's House,E ter- ton Gardens, London, S.W., under date May 31st, stating that on th,, previous Tuesday the stench from Messrs Long and Son's Tannery was very bad. He understood the Council's Medical Officer hal vioited the Tannery, and he asked for his r,,port. Waiting on the same subject. Mr Lewis W Reynolds, Millington House, Thelwall, Warrington, under date May 31st, complained that the nuisance from Mr Long's tannery was very bad on the firat three days of the week, particularly on Tuesday, the 27th May, when the windows of his house had to be kept shut all day, and his wife could not walk in the garden as the smell was everywhere, and made her feel quite ill. He feared that Ithe drainage works now being carried on in the lane would not put an end to this nuisance,though the cover- ing in of the stinking ditch would be a great improve- naent. The ventilator which had been placed upon the culvert would be continually discharging foul air on a level with the windows of the adjacent houses, and the tannery settling tanks, when being cleaned, or pumped our, as had been the case that week, would cause a dreadful stench which could be noticed even a mile laway, and residents near the Thalwall Station on Wed- nesday spoke to him about the bad smell from the tannery, He had himself when at the station, recog- nized the smell, so they might imagine it was pretty bad about there.

Dr Adams said that as the surveyor was prevented from going with him on the date named he went him- self. Ns noticed there was a smell of sewage which was not a tannery ortlsll at all. Itemanated from a two faot sewer which came from Mr Naylor's own property. The workingmen stated that they had smelt the sewage matter and that the rain had washed it down. The smell was due to the sub soil-be;ng disturbaJ. He had no report to make on the matter. Admiral Jones-Parry stated that no water could coins down the sewer mentioned. On the Thursday there was a most disgusting stench. On the Tdesday Mr Swinton was there and want over Mr Naylor's premises to find the stench but failed. It could not come from Mr Naylor's beeause his place was closed and the drain had been examined. He expected a fuller report from the Medical Officer than had been given. Dr Adams said that when the rain came down it went through Ur Naylor's settling tank which rought the efluent down the pipe. Admiral Jones-Parry : There should be no real diffi- culty in tracing where the smell comes from. Would it not be as well to offer a reward of £5O to anyone who could tell us? (Laughter.) Mr Swinton stated that the nuisance came from Mr Naylor's tank. The sewage came down the two foot pipe. The tank overflowed in Mr Naylor's absence, it was not attendad to and there was consequently a lot ofilsediment at the bottom. The recent heavy rains ' washed down the sewage from the gardener's cottage, the stable house and the coachman's cottage. There was nowhere for the top sewage to go. Mr Farrington. the iaspntor, Waq 11191 of opinion that Mr Naylor's sewag,e was to blame for the smell. _

Mr Edwards tlio-ught a-t-t‘e-r—ws a st-rm in a teapot. Mr Naylor wag really to blamo because the 8111Pil arose final his own sewage, Dr Adams, in reply to a queqion, thought that the ventilating shaft near Mr Naylors property bad nothing to do with the nuisance at all.

THE EDUCATION BILL. The Clerk reported that at the last meeting of the Council a circular letter was submitted from the Rural District Councils' Association asking for their opinion on several points in regard to the proposed Education Bill. A committee was appointed to coneider the matter and unanimouely arrived at the following replies to the various questions :—(1) Whether your Council approve of the additional experre which will be incurred in maintaining the voluntary schools being thrown upon the rates. It is uncertain what this expense will be, but it has been sufre.ested that the rate will probably be from 4d to lid ; or, whether your Council think that the necessary funds or a poltion of them should be provided by the Imperial Exchequer. Reply : The Council are of the opinion that the whole of the additional expense which will be incurred in maintaining the voluntary schools should be provided for by the Imperial Exchequer. (1) Whether you think the Bill should remain permissive or whether it should be made compulsory. Reply • The Bill should be made compulsory. (3) Whether you think that Rural District Councils with a population of,sey,over 20,000 or Oven to 10,000 should be allowed to beeonee the Eluce- tion Authority themselves. Reply : Rural District Councils with a copulation of 20,000 should be allowed to become the Education Authority themselves. (4) Whether you think that Rural District Ceuncilis should have a voice in the appointment of the Education Com- mittee. Reply : If Rural District Councils with a popu- lation of 20,000 Piro not allowed to booome the Education Authority themselves, they should have a voice in the appointment of the Education Committee, and all other Rural District Councils with'a less population should have a voice in such appointment for their district.

div.head: EDUCATION BILL. Animated Discussion in the Town Council.
div.p: THE EDUCATION BILL. Animated Discussion in the Town Council.
Religious Differences. "Desirable Amendments" Recom- mended.

At the Town Council meeting on Tuesday even- ing, a discussion arose on the minutes of the Museum Committee which contained resolutions regarding the Government Education Bill. The Committee hail resolved :—(1) That the Town Council be recommended to express general appro- val of the prin 3iples of the Government Education Bill, and willingness to accept the responsibilities which would devolve upon the local authority, in the belief that it would thereby be enabled to de- velop and improve all kinds of education within the borough. (2) That the following amendments in details are desirable ;—Clause 5, the application of part 3 to be compulsory. Clause 8 (1) it, The managers to be appointed by the local authority to be less than one-half the whole number. Clause 8 (2) to apply to the whole of the Act. Clause 13 (3) to be deleted. It was resolved. that copies of the above resolutions be forwarded to the First Lord of the Treasury, the Vice-President of the Board of Education, Mr Pierpoint, M.P., and the Association of Municipal Corporations. Alderman Moxics proposed the cliffirmation of the minutes, and alluding to the Education Bill said there was a good deal in the Bill which he did not altogether like, hut there seemed to have been so much difficulty in getting an alteration at all in educational matters that he thought it was better to take the Bill and make the best of it. The Council would remember that he moved a petition in favour of the passing of the Bill, but it having already passed its second reading it was not of much importance that they did not get what they wanted. The important thing was to get altera- tions made in-committee, and these recommenda- tions of the committee were designed to improve the Bill. Proceeding to amplify the recommenda- tion Alderman Monks said in reference to the second that clause 8, section 1 sub-section 3 pro- vided that the members of the committee of management of each school nominated by the Council should not exceed one 3rd. This seemed rather a small portion if the control was to be effective and toe number might, as they suggested, be increased until the managers appointed by the Council were one less than half. That was giving the existing managers a majority of one. Clause 13, which they wanted deleted dealt with the method of keeping and auditing the accounts. It was provided that the accounts should be audited by the Local Government Board auditors, and it seemed to them batter that the accounts should be kept under the system adopted under the Muni- cipal Corporations Act—that was Riving the borough auditors power to deal with the matter. lie thought it would be an advantage to have the accounts audited along with the other accounts of the Corporation..

Councillor A J 'JOLLEY seconded the motion. The DEPUTY-MAYOR said it was net his intention to move an amendment, but he had one or two sugges- tions to make. They did not wieh,he was sure, to enter into any sectarian dispute whatever. Sc far as they could, those of them with strong views as to the injus- tice proposed to be dealt cut to them were prepared to confine the discussion to these points which concerned the municipalisation of the question of education, and leave sectarian difficultiee to the Howie of Commons. Before coming to the suggestions he had to make he felt bound te just point out what, to his mind, were the essential points of difference between the Corporation Bill and the Bill of the Gavernmene became some of them had been held to be ioconsietent owing to the the fact that they were prepared to support the Cor- poration Bill while they were not prepared to give the same amount of support to the Government Bill In the first place, he ssid, the Corporation Bill provided merely for the erection and maintenance of such addi- tional schools as the Educetioa Department considered necessary to supply the accommodation which the pre- sent schoolspiwere not equal to supply. On the other hand, the Government Bill, provided part 3 was adopted —and its compulsory adoption seemed probable—placed the financial responsibility attaching to all schools, so far as their equipment and maintenance for teaching pur- poses was concerned, upon the local authority—the Corporation—and the burden of such responsibility would fall upon the ratepayers. In reference to the Cor- poration Bel, such additional schools would have been undenominational in character, and therfore no restric- tions as to religious beliefs would have been imposed on the teaching staff in any way whatever. The Government Bill provided for the strict maintenance of the degnini- national character of the vo.untsry schoola, and thereby provided a weapon of immease magnitude which might be used by clerics and laymen of strong sectarian views, r. for the exclusion from the teaching profession, either as pupil teachers or masters of all such as did not hold the particular religious opinions which were espoused by the school managers. Such exclusion in a elate and , rate-3upported profession was ur3just and would, he trusted not be persisted in. lie had some hope because I he recognised with very p,reat gratitude the fair-minded I utterance of the Archbishop of Canterbury last I week. Ho had stated as many other men had stated that there was undoubtedly a very just sue- p;cion on the part of the None-infer:Lists that their interests under the Bill were not sufficiently safeguarded as they out to be and it was sugeeeed that a confer- ence should be held at which the leaders of the various religious denominations wou'd meet together in the hope of arriving at some fair and equitable adjustment of the matters embodied in the Bill. He had every reason to believe that some such proposal would Corns into effectual operation before very lone. (Rear, hear.) The third point he wished to refer to was that the Corpora- tion under their Bill would have had entire control of the schools they erected, whereas under the Government Bill, the Corporations instead of being entitled to a majority e'represens- Cation on the management of these public elementary schools, which except for the fabric of the buildings will be entirely epuipped by public money. was only to have a representation not exceeding one third of the manage- ment. Could anything be more unfair or more sulever- , sive of the old well-tried and well-proved maxim that , tax etion and representation ought to bear fair compari- I son one with the other. With reference to the I constitution of the educational authority he would ' suggest that the Corporation have ample powers con- ferred upon them so that no child should suffer from the religioue convictions of its parente. If some ' arrangement could be made by which theSootch system could be introduced into Eagland he would he glad. In Scotland teem was no religious difficulty whatever because the child of a Unitarian, a Roman Catholic, a Presbyterian or Nonconformist of any denomination could be taught its own particular religioua opinions by the clergyman or minister he the school which was provided by the State and supported by the rates. It was a matter of great reeret that England was so far behind Scoeland and Wales in these important matters. He wished to amplify the requisi- tions of the Museum Committee in one or two reipecta. With reference to clause ft, be would suggest that toe committee's amendment be altered so as to read " The managers to be appointed by the local authority to he not less than one-half the whole number." Ha did not ask for a majerity but he thought the Corporation which had to bear the ultimete responsibility for the financial difficulty, after the sub- scrip,ion list, which wee a great factor in voluntary schools, was abolished, was entitled to half of the repre- sentation in the management of the various schools. He would also suggest that an additional recommendation he made by the Museum Ceminittee"ehat the opeciallaid grant of 5s per head at present paid to denominational schools only, be discontinued or else extended to all public elementary sehoeisi recognised be the educational authority of the locality." He made these two sagge4- tinos in the desire that their own fairness would carry conviction. Be had endeavoured in stating the case for the Nonconformists—he wars afraid in a very inadeqUato and insufficient manner—to recognise that that was haedly the proper piece to (-Recess sectarian di ff irences but rather how to apply them to the best advalt age. (Hear, hear). Alderman MONKS said personally he had no objtion to the incorporation of the suggestions named in the recommendations of the Museum Committee. So far as the special aid grant was concerned he would prefer it to be paid to all schools alike and thug make it general. Councillor SMETEILY HST remarked that the Council decided to leave the matter in the hands of the Ineeum Committee- The committee now submitted their re- port and he thought it ought to tin accepted. He Was surprised that stress had been laid on the amount of voluntary subscriptions that would have to he paid by the local authority if the Bill pimed. In many eases they were very small indeed. At People's College School for instance there were no voluntary subscriptions becanee the fees and grants paid the expenses. Alderman MONKS denied that this was so and minted out that the managers had to rely on subscriptions as , well.

Councillor SMETHURST ( continuing) said the volun taly subscriptions in connection with Trinity gehnOl were aq Hiewe during the last three years :-1899 £3B, 1900 £3O and 1901 £27 10s. In connection with S. Jamey's school the voluntary suhverintions were 1899 £5 ; 1900 £l7 89 6d ; 1901 £2O Is. It would bo seen that the voluntary subecriptions were really very small and vet this was one of the things which the Noncon- formists, who were in a minorkty, were troubling about. . _
Alderman Dorman : In a minority ? You are wrong in your figures, Councillor SMETIIIIRST : I am quoting from Dr Gornall's report.

showed, at all events that one half the nation was at variance entirely with the provisions now being discussed in the House of C 0021310113 (" No, No. He believed he had shown conclusively that at least one half of the nation held the Bill was unwise and im- politic. (" No ") and he agreed with the sugges- tion that there snould be an opportunity for discussion, so as to evolve a proper, good sound system of national education from it. He must confess that he did net approve of the resolution before the Council, He ex- pected, when he left the meeting of the Museum Com- mittee, that they would have a report which they could have discussed in. detail. He did not see how they could do anything with the minutes before them. If they were passed that night they would be passed not by the thoughtful section of the Council. ("Oh, oh"). Councillor A J JOLLEY, as seconder of the minutes, expressed his willingness to accept the suggestions of the Deputy-Mayor. He wished to discuss the matter in 1 the same temperate spirit that the Deputy-Mayor adopted, and which he thought it would have besa ad- vantage sus if one or two other members had followed. There seemed to be a misapprehension in the minds of some members on two or taree points. He admitted,as one or two of the speakers had said, that they should never come to an agreement, but he was under the impression that in a democratic country they hoped to get to the region of satisf sc- tory results by further discussion and conference. He considered that to attempt to stifle any discussion was not very wise. With regard to the amount of Con- trol to be exercised by the local authority, he submitted that anyone who read carefully section 3 would see clearly that as regarded secular instruction, the local authority would have absolute power, and managers would be bound to carry out the directions of the authority. It was a matter of vital importance to the nation, and they all wanted i to see secular instruction improved all round. He was prepared to figot for that as long 33 he had any energy left to fight at all. In regard to the subscrip- tions to valuntary schools, he submitted that the ' majority of the schools would have ta raise large sums ' by voluntary eff srt under the Bill than they had to raise at the present time. ("No.") He was only speaking as far as his knowledge weat, and he know a great many schools in Lancashire. With regard to the aid grant, Councillor Jolley said he agreed with the sugges- tion of Sir A Rollitc in the matter. He also pointed out that the grant wail I not be paid to the managers of voluntary schools, but to the 10E11 authority. He did not wish to say very much about the religious difficulty. So far as he could see it would be impossible to devise anything more scrupulously fair than the clauses of the Bill which dealt with the deumninational difficulty. He ventured to think that one or two members of the Council who had spokea had not taken the trouble to read over clause 4,0 r if they had, they must have read it in such a perfunctory way that they had not understood it. As an expression of opinion, differ- jag from Councillor F R Rebuts, he ventured to say that the Bill was a large and statesmanlike measure— the best measure dealing with education which had been before the country in the present generation,—and that if faced facts. However strongly some people might desire to see purely secular education, they had to recognize the fact that there was a very large number of people—and he ventured Co ea s not the least thoughtful —who believed tiat purely secular education would lead to vere great trouble, and would be little less than a national disaster. fie really failed to see how, if we were to have denominational education at all—they could have it conducted on fairer lines than were sug- gested in this Bill. The old conscience clauses would also remain in operation.

In conclusion he said he ventured to say that the members nf the Government responsible for the drafting of the Bill had approached it in a large and statesounliko manner. The Bill enabled the religious difficulty to be satisfactorily dealt with. The Tows CLERK sail he had received from the Secre- tary of the Association of Municipal Corporations a report en the Bill, submitted by the Council of the Association. All the recommendations contained in the resolutiol of the Miseum Committee, autl one of those proposed by the Deputy-Mayor had been agreed to by the Association.

_ The DEPUTY-MAYOR said he recognized the probability that the Bill in some form would be passed by the Government, and it was his desire to mahe it as accept- able as it could be made to those members of the Council who differed horn some of its main provisions. He did not consider that any member of the Council who was a Noaconformist—as he wai himself, and proud to proclaim the fact—was in any sense sacrificinr principle by supporting proposals which wouldliva him something more than the original proposal suggested. Alderman MINKS did not agree with the opinion which had been expressed that the Council was wasting time by discussing the Bill. On the contrary be though the Council had done a great deal of good in causing the members and also members. of the public to read the Bill and think the matter carefully over. He pointed out that the Manchester Corporation bad considered the Bill and had embodied in their suggestions those which the Musuem Committee recommencleu for adoption by the Council. There were ether bodieS which had thought fit to act unon similar tines. It the Bill were passed, and the schools of Warrington were carried on in the same lines on which they wen carried on to- day, it did not necessarily mean much additional fitiancill responsibility to be put on tho shoulders of this ratepayers, but if they were going to start with a liberal scale of salaries, and all sorts of improvements and extravagancies, is would not take very much to run up a big bill and that would cause regret to those who had advocated any sues changes. He considered that the fact that the grant would be paid to the local authority indicated that the authority would have con- trol of the 'schools, and if they were not managed in accordance with the regulations that the authority laid down, could stop the funds and in that way exercise very efficient control. He was not prepared to with- draw the commitoee's resolutions. On a vote being taken the resolution was carried, only Councillor F R Roberta voting against it.

RUNCORN BOARD OF GUARDIANS.

The fortnightly meeting of this authority was held at Dutton on Tuesday. Present :—Mr A R Norman, (in the chair), Messrs S Taylor, T Lea, J Douglas, the mem- bers of the Rural District Council with Messrs G F Ashton (clerk), and W E Rough (assistant clerk). RE-ADJUSTMENT OF THE COUTY RATE BASIS.

Mr Reginald Potts, clerk to the Cheshire County Coun- cil, wrote under date 25:h May, notifying the Board that the County rate basis and assessable value had been revised for the following parishes :—Acton Grange, County rate basis, £7247; assessable value, £484 ; Bartiny,ton, £876. £613 ; Clift3n, £3,535. £3,564 ; Dutton, £9.172. £7.869 ; Grappenhall. £8,805, £7,797 ; Relsby, £10,121, £9,212 ; Kingswood, £2,380, £1,560 ; Latchford Without, £2,489, £2.381 ; Norley, £4,677, £3,544 ; Norton, £7,020, £5,963 ; Preston-o'-th'-flill. £4,264, £3,652 ; Stockton Heath, £9,397, £9,320 ; Walton Inferior, £5,058, £4,729. Mr Ashton explained Zhat the readjustment was the result of clrrespladence with Mr Potts. The basis of the poor rate bad been altered, and this necessitated the revision.

PROP MED SANATORIUM FOR CONSUMPTIVES. Mr Reginald Yotts, cleek co the County Council, in a circular letter to the Board, stated that aa the Council was of opinion that the establishment of a sanatorium or sanatoria for the treatment of consumptives would be for the benefit of the County, he was instructed to invite representatives of all the sanitary autoorittes in the administrative county and Boards of G aarajaas to a conference wit a the Isolation Hospitals Acts sub-com- mittee of the Public Health Committee of this Council, with a view to steps being taken for the establishment of such a sanatorium or sanatoria. He should accord- ingly be glad to be informed in due course whether the , Board would appoint say two representatives to attend the proposed conference, and if so, to be furnished with the names thereof. The Chairman stated that a conference, at which he I was present, had been held on the, subject and he was pleased to see that the County C.)uocil were again bringing the matter forward. Mr Woodward said that the right course had teen 1 taken by the County Council in proposing to consider the iprovision of a sanatorium for consumptives. A 1 single Union or combination of Unions could not deal with the matter and it was really the work of the County Council. He proposed that Messrs Norman and Williams be appointed as representatives. Mr Taylor seconded and the motion was passed.

PROPOSED LBOLITION OF OVERSEERS. The Weardale oion forwarded copy of resolution adopted by them, asking for tho support of the Runcorn Board, to the effect that the office of overseer ought to be .bolished and the duties taken over by the Assess- ment Committee provision being made that each parish be represented on the Committee. This arrangement would prevent confusion and maladministration. The Assistant Ouerseer should be appointed and paid by the Guardians who IlTUld be directly responsible to the Assessment Committee, Referred to the Parliamentary Committee, PINS NCE. Mr Woodward reported that the outpayments were as follows .—Runcorn, £BO ; Frodsham, £23 ; Bud worth £2B. The report was approved.

As Ben Wilson nart ny now apparently resigned himself entirely into the hands of Providence, he only shook his head sorrowfully; Adams was impressed with the truth of his friend's statement but did not see what he could add to it; Mr. Short alone still seemed to be equal to the emergency. "Inspector Granger," he said, " I think there is ono fact in our friend's explanation that eau be proved. If both shafts of the trap are found to be cracked; that the mare has been down is the only reasonable way to account for it. Perhaps also the mare bears signs about her 2" "That she do," cried the farmer, "I noticed fresh mud on her hocks myself." " Well then we may say without doubt there has been an upsetting as Ben Wilson affirms," he con- tinued, "in the place where you found the grass cut up." The Inspector nodded as granted. "What will this account for? Firstly for his lateness at Red Ash, again forhis appearance, also it provides a passable explanation, under the circumstances, of his hiding from us what, to put it bluntly, his ob- stinacy had resulted in. Then as to the stake, most likely holes are left both where he pulled it from, and also where stuck in to hold the gate." "Certainly any man can see 'em who goes to the place," said Ben, who was beginning to take an in- terest in life again. " Then as to their having made friends as Ben Wilson here tells us, perhaps there were witnesses I" Mr. Short proceeded. "Certainly," cried Ben with increasing liveliness, "we met at the White Hart, you've on'y to send down the village to Sim Wilkins there, he was driving with me that day, we had three sacks of the best oats, I—" Mr. Short was compelled to cut the hay merchant short in his restored vivacity. "Then compare a powerful fellow like Tom Reynolds with our friend here, it is impossible that they could have had a struggle, of this the dead man's face is also a proof. W ilsons' disordered appearance is then more evidence of a trap accident, and consequently of his innocence than guilt. Lastly, consider the improbability of it all, the relations on which we stand; do you have sufficient grounds to justify such a step as immediate arrest ?" Mr. Short's clear-beaded views had great effect on the Inspector, but he walked and nodded, and tripped the furniture, considering for some time be- fore making any remark. Then he opened the win- dow and gazed pointedly at several policemen who had returned from the search party scattered about the country side. "Ben Wilson," he said, "I must beg of you for your own sake, to remain in this room until I return." He then left the house. - The Inspector's face had lightened considerably when in an hour's space he re-appeared "I have been making the inquiries Mr. Short suggested, and others of my own, and have come to the conclusion that the unpleasant duty I feared is unnecessary. I can't tell you, Ben, of the relief it is." They shook hands and Ben, cheerfully but in all seriousness observed. "After all, Granger, my lad, if ever you want to arrest me again, you've only got to call round at my place, that is in office hours, of course, this seeming to the hay merchant to put the finishing touch of satisfaction to an awkward. episode. The doer of the crime was never discovered by the police , poor Tom Reynolds lies still unavenged by the majesty of the law; his murderer goes at large, and takes his place among other men as of yore. Further evidence completely exonerated Ben Wilson from any suspicion. principally that of a labourer who at a distance had watched the whole crossing of the trap through the gully, including the fall of the old mare. Can anyone elucidate the mystery? Well, Farmer Adams grows thoughtful and silent when gossips bring up the now long past tale. He remembers a scene in the wood-shed some six months after. " Come, chop away there, Bill," the farmer said to his man, watching him cut firewood for the house- " Ha, ha," laughed Bill Goose, it took three or four of his nerveless ill-directed blows to sever a branch which would have yielded to one if the twiia cunning of head and hand had been present. "Ever heard anything of little dog' Bill," he asked idly. 800--00, little dog' left poor Bill," the wood chopper wailed in answer! The farmer's curiosity stirred him to an experi- ment. The man was dead, he thought, it could do no harm. "Do ye know, Bill, they say she was shot, and they do say it was Tom Rey—" the farmer broke suddenly off, for an alarming change had come over Bill at his words. His stalwart form stiffened to its great height, he raised the axe on high with a swing, and brought it down on a large branch, which fell cleft in two. Some memory rose strongly within that half-formed brain. Ho wever the spasm passed almost as rapidly as it had risen, but the fanner returning to the house, went straight to a certain cupboard, and lifted out a gun which bad lain there since Bill Goose had brought it back from Watkins of the Grange on the fatal day. He stood a long time over that gun re- flecting. deeply. At length he bestirred to get a piece of rag, and muttering to himself " Poor idiot, he didn't know no better, what good would it do !" cleansed the butt from some dark stains and several red hairs that clung to it. Thus did Bill Goose have his slate wiped of all ugly mark, and thus was his freedom continued to him, so that his jovial Ha ha was for many years a merry, if at first a startling element in the village and district life. Still at times Farmer Adams would let his eyes rest on him in . a long and meditative stare, terminating unfailingly in a compassionate head- shake, together with " Poor idiot, what good woul4. it do !" "What good indeed !" we can only Was. That veteran salt Admiral of the fleet Sir Barry Reppel, who was received in audience by the King on Saturday, enters upon his ninety-fourth year on Saturday' in next week. Sir Rarry, who has just returned from journey to Singapr re—an achievement which at his age is little short of a marvel—has lived in no fewer than five reigns, and the torthcomiog, Coronation will be the fourth which he can say he remembers, for he was a boy of eleven when Geotge IV. came to the throne.—" West- minster Gazetts."
